observable or active projection.

Definition 2.1 — Future-active retained
consequence
A retained state m is future-active at x if there exists another
retained state \tilde m\in\mathcal M such that
\Pi_1^x(x,m)
\neq
\Pi_1^x(x,\tilde m).

 Thus retention is not defined merely by storage. It is defined
by future influence.

2.3 Retained-State Relevance
Proposition 2.1 — Equivalent tests for onestep relevance
For fixed x, the following are equivalent:
1. m is future-active relative to some \tilde m.
2. There exists u\in\mathcal U such that
F(x,m,u)\neq F(x,\tilde m,u).
3. The maps
F_{x,m}:u\mapsto F(x,m,u)
and
F_{x,\tilde m}:u\mapsto F(x,\tilde m,u)
are not identical.
4. The projected one-step possibility sets differ for at least
one common admissible-input model.

Proof
If statement 2 holds, then at least one output under the same
admissible input differs, so the two input-to-state maps are
not identical; hence 3 follows.
If the maps differ, there exists some input at which their
outputs differ, so 3 implies 2.

 If 2 holds, then the systems possess different active-state
successors under that input. Under the common-input
interpretation of the possibility map, their one-step future
structures differ, giving 1.
Conversely, if the possibility sets differ, then some successor
belongs to one set but not the other. Therefore the underlying
maps cannot agree on every admissible input, establishing 2.
∎

2.4 Inert Storage
Definition 2.2 — Dynamically inert retained
state
A retained variable is dynamically inert over a domain
D\subseteq\Omega if
F(x,m,u)=F(x,\tilde m,u)
for all
x\in D,
\qquad
m,\tilde m\in\mathcal M,
\qquad
u\in\mathcal U.
In this case, the active dynamics are independent of retained
state on D.

 Theorem 2.2 — Inert-storage elimination
If m is dynamically inert over D, then the active-state
dynamics reduce to a memory-independent map
x_{n+1}
=
\bar F(x_n,u_n)
for trajectories remaining in D.

Proof
Because F is independent of the retained-state argument on
D, choose any fixed m_0\in\mathcal M and define
\bar F(x,u)=F(x,m_0,u).
For every m,
F(x,m,u)=F(x,m_0,u)=\bar F(x,u).
Therefore the active-state recursion is
x_{n+1}=\bar F(x_n,u_n).
The retained variable may continue to evolve internally, but
it does not influence the active trajectory while the state
remains in D. ∎
This theorem formalizes the difference between stored
history and future-active memory.

 2.5 Multi-Step Reachability
Define the n-step reachable set recursively:
\Pi_0(z)=\{z\},
and
\Pi_{n+1}(z)
=
\bigcup_{y\in\Pi_n(z)}
\left\{
T(y,u):u\in\mathcal U
\right\}.
The active-state projection is
\Pi_n^x(z)
=
\operatorname{pr}_\Omega\Pi_n(z).
The total reachable set is
\Pi_\infty(z)
=
\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}\Pi_n(z).

Definition 2.3 — n-step retained influence
Two retained states m,\tilde m have distinguishable n-step
influence at active state x if

 \Pi_n^x(x,m)
\neq
\Pi_n^x(x,\tilde m).

Lemma 2.3 — One-step influence implies
finite-horizon influence
If
\Pi_1^x(x,m)
\neq
\Pi_1^x(x,\tilde m),
then the two retained states are distinguishable at some finite
horizon.

Proof
The result holds immediately with horizon n=1. ∎
The reverse need not hold. Two retained states may produce
identical one-step active outcomes but differ later because
their internal retained-state updates are different.

2.6 Delayed Retained Influence
Proposition 2.4 — Hidden memory can act
after a delay
There exist systems satisfying

 \Pi_1^x(x,m)
=
\Pi_1^x(x,\tilde m)
but
\Pi_2^x(x,m)
\neq
\Pi_2^x(x,\tilde m).

Construction
Let
\Omega=\mathbb R,
\qquad
\mathcal M=\mathbb R,
\qquad
\mathcal U=\{0\}.
Define
x_{n+1}=m_n,
m_{n+1}=m_n.
Now choose the initial active state x=0, with m=1 and \tilde
m=-1.
Actually, under this definition the one-step active states
already differ. To create a one-step delay, instead define
x_{n+1}=0,

 m_{n+1}=m_n,
for the first stage, and augment the system with a clock
variable q\in\{0,1\}:
x_{n+1}
=
q_nm_n,
m_{n+1}=m_n,
q_{n+1}=1.
Starting with q_0=0, both retained states produce
x_1=0.
At the next step,
x_2=m_1,
so m=1 gives x_2=1, while \tilde m=-1 gives x_2=-1.
Therefore one-step active possibility is identical while twostep possibility differs. ∎
This shows why memory cannot always be assessed through
immediate output alone.

2.7 Augmented-State Markov
Closure

 A system with history dependence may appear nonMarkovian when described only by x_n.
Suppose
x_{n+1}
=
H(x_n,x_{n-1},\ldots,x_{n-r+1},u_n).
Define the augmented state
z_n
=
(x_n,x_{n-1},\ldots,x_{n-r+1}).

Theorem 2.5 — Finite-history Markov
embedding
Every deterministic system with finite memory length r can
be represented as a first-order Markov recursion on an
augmented state space.

Proof
Define
z_n
=
(x_n,x_{n-1},\ldots,x_{n-r+1}).
Then

 z_{n+1}
=
\Bigl(
H(x_n,\ldots,x_{n-r+1},u_n),
x_n,
x_{n-1},
\ldots,
x_{n-r+2}
\Bigr).
Therefore there exists a map
\widehat T
such that
z_{n+1}
=
\widehat T(z_n,u_n).
The next augmented state depends only on the present
augmented state and input, not on earlier values outside z_n.
Hence the augmented recursion is first-order Markov. ∎

Corollary 2.6 — Memory can be represented
structurally
Finite temporal dependence can always be rewritten as
present-state dependence on an enlarged state space.

 This does not eliminate memory physically or conceptually.
It locates memory inside the present mathematical state.

2.8 Possibility Transformation
Let the current possibility structure be
\mathcal P_n=\Pi_1(z_n).
After one realized input u_n, the state becomes
z_{n+1}=T(z_n,u_n),
and the new possibility structure is
\mathcal P_{n+1}
=
\Pi_1(z_{n+1}).
Thus the possibility-update operator is
\mathfrak P:
(z_n,u_n)
\mapsto
\Pi_1(T(z_n,u_n)).
Symbolically,
\mathcal P_n
\xrightarrow{\Sigma_n}
A_n
\xrightarrow{\Gamma}
M_{n+1}

 \longrightarrow
\mathcal P_{n+1}.
Here:
•
•
•
•

\Sigma_n selects an admissible transition;
A_n is the realized interaction;
\Gamma updates retained consequence;
\mathcal P_{n+1} is the transformed future possibility
set.

2.9 Selection as a Map
Let
\Pi_1(z)
be nonempty.
A deterministic selection operator is a choice function
\Sigma:
\mathcal Z
\rightarrow
\mathcal U
such that
\Sigma(z)\in\mathcal U.
The resulting closed-loop transition is

 T_\Sigma(z)
=
T(z,\Sigma(z)).
If selection is made directly from possible successor states,
write
\widehat\Sigma(z)\in\Pi_1(z).

Lemma 2.7 — Selection induces a trajectory
Given an initial state z_0 and a deterministic selection
operator \Sigma, there exists a uniquely determined recursive
trajectory whenever T is a function.

Proof
Define
z_{n+1}
=
T(z_n,\Sigma(z_n)).
Because T and \Sigma are functions, z_{n+1} is uniquely
determined from z_n. Induction defines a unique sequence
for every n\ge0. ∎

2.10 Stochastic Selection
Let

 K(\cdot\mid z)
be a Markov kernel assigning a probability distribution over
admissible successor states.
Then the next-state distribution is
\mu_{n+1}(B)
=
\int_{\mathcal Z}
K(B\mid z)\,d\mu_n(z).
The retained state is future-active probabilistically if
changing it changes the transition kernel:
K(\cdot\mid x,m)
\neq
K(\cdot\mid x,\tilde m).

Proposition 2.8 — Probabilistic retained
influence
If there exists a measurable set B\subseteq\mathcal Z such
that
K(B\mid x,m)
\neq
K(B\mid x,\tilde m),
then the retained states m and \tilde m induce distinct onestep probability laws.

 Proof
Probability measures are equal if and only if they agree on all
measurable sets. Since they differ on B, the one-step laws are
distinct. ∎
Thus retained consequence can alter not only reachable states
but also their probabilities.

2.11 Constraint-Dependent
Possibility
Let admissibility be determined by
C:\mathcal Z\times\mathcal U\rightarrow\{0,1\}.
Define the admissible input set
\mathcal U_C(z)
=
\{u\in\mathcal U:C(z,u)=1\}.
Then
\Pi_1^C(z)
=
\{T(z,u):u\in\mathcal U_C(z)\}.
Retained consequence may influence future possibility
through either:
1. the transition law T;

 2. the admissibility law C;
3. both.

Theorem 2.9 — Two mechanisms of
possibility change
Let z=(x,m) and \tilde z=(x,\tilde m). If either
T(z,u)\neq T(\tilde z,u)
for some commonly admissible u, or
\mathcal U_C(z)\neq\mathcal U_C(\tilde z),
then retained state can alter the constrained one-step
possibility structure.

Proof
In the first case, a common admissible input produces
different successor states, so the transition image changes
unless the difference is exactly compensated by another input
image.
In the second case, the domains over which successor states
are generated differ. Therefore the candidate transition family
differs. Whenever the removed or added input generates a
successor not duplicated by another admissible input, the
possibility sets differ.
Thus retained consequence can reshape possibility by
altering state response, action admissibility, or both. ∎

 The qualification regarding duplicated successor states is
necessary: different controls can sometimes generate
identical successor sets.

2.12 Strong Possibility Influence
To avoid ambiguity from duplicate images, define the
transition relation
\mathscr R_z
=
\{(u,T(z,u)):u\in\mathcal U_C(z)\}.

Definition 2.4 — Strong future influence
Retained states m and \tilde m have different strong future
influence at x if
\mathscr R_{(x,m)}
\neq
\mathscr R_{(x,\tilde m)}.
This preserves both admissible actions and their
consequences rather than comparing only the resulting state
set.

Theorem 2.10 — Exact criterion for strong
future influence

 For fixed active state x,
\mathscr R_{(x,m)}
=
\mathscr R_{(x,\tilde m)}
if and only if:
1. the admissible input sets are identical; and
2. the transition outputs agree for every admissible input.

Proof
If the relations are equal, their projections onto the input
coordinate are equal, so the admissible input sets coincide.
Equality of ordered pairs then gives equal transition outputs
for each input.
Conversely, if the domains coincide and all input-output
pairs coincide, then the relations are identical. ∎

2.13 Persistence Filter
Let
\mathcal H_n
=
(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_n)
denote interaction history.
A compression map

 C_n:\mathcal H_n\rightarrow\mathcal M
produces the retained state
m_n=C_n(\mathcal H_n).
A persistence filter is a map
F_P:\mathcal M\rightarrow\mathcal M
that preserves, suppresses, or transforms retained
components.
A simple linear example is
m_{n+1}
=
Am_n+B\varphi(A_n),
where:
• A controls retention and decay;
• B\varphi(A_n) encodes the new interaction
consequence.

2.14 Linear Persistence Recursion
Consider
m_{n+1}
=
Am_n+b_n.
Iterating gives

 m_n
=
A^nm_0
+
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
A^{n-1-k}b_k.

Lemma 2.11 — Exact persistence
decomposition
The retained state equals the surviving initial state plus the
accumulated, time-weighted contributions of later
interactions.

Proof
For n=1,
m_1=Am_0+b_0.
Assume
m_n
=
A^nm_0
+
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}A^{n-1-k}b_k.
Then
\begin{aligned}
m_{n+1}

 &=
Am_n+b_n\\
&=
A^{n+1}m_0
+
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}A^{n-k}b_k
+b_n\\
&=
A^{n+1}m_0
+
\sum_{k=0}^{n}A^{n-k}b_k.
\end{aligned}
Thus the formula holds by induction. ∎

2.15 Decay and Retention
Theorem 2.12 — Stable linear forgetting
Suppose
\|A\|\le\rho<1
and b_n=0. Then
\|m_n\|
\le
\rho^n\|m_0\|,
so

 m_n\rightarrow0.

Proof
From
m_n=A^nm_0,
submultiplicativity gives
\|m_n\|
\le
\|A\|^n\|m_0\|
\le
\rho^n\|m_0\|.
Since 0\le\rho<1, \rho^n\to0. ∎

Theorem 2.13 — Bounded-input boundedmemory result
Suppose
\|A\|\le\rho<1
and
\|b_n\|\le B.
Then
\|m_n\|
\le

 \rho^n\|m_0\|
+
\frac{B(1-\rho^n)}{1-\rho},
and therefore
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\|m_n\|
\le
\frac{B}{1-\rho}.

Proof
Using the exact decomposition,
\begin{aligned}
\|m_n\|
&\le
\|A^nm_0\|
+
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
\|A^{n-1-k}b_k\|\\
&\le
\rho^n\|m_0\|
+
B\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\rho^j\\
&=
\rho^n\|m_0\|
+
B\frac{1-\rho^n}{1-\rho}.
\end{aligned}

 Taking the limit superior gives the result. ∎
This theorem formalizes a balance between reinforcement
and decay.

2.16 Persistence Threshold Model
Consider the scalar model
\dot w
=
D_+(t)-D_-(t)-\delta w+\eta(t),
\qquad
\delta>0.
Here:
• D_+ is constructive drive;
• D_- is destructive drive;
• \delta w is proportional decay;
• \eta is disturbance.
Assume constants
D_+(t)\ge d_+,
\qquad
D_-(t)\le d_-,
\qquad
\eta(t)\ge-\varepsilon.
Then

 \dot w
\ge
d_+-d_--\varepsilon-\delta w.
Define
w_{\mathrm{eq}}
=
\frac{d_+-d_--\varepsilon}{\delta}.

Theorem 2.14 — Lower persistence bound
If d_+-d_--\varepsilon>0, then
w(t)
\ge
w_{\mathrm{eq}}
+
\bigl(w(0)-w_{\mathrm{eq}}\bigr)e^{-\delta t}.

Proof
Compare w with the solution y of
\dot y
=
d_+-d_--\varepsilon-\delta y,
\qquad
y(0)=w(0).
The explicit solution is

 y(t)
=
w_{\mathrm{eq}}
+
\bigl(w(0)-w_{\mathrm{eq}}\bigr)e^{-\delta t}.
Since
\dot w+\delta w
\ge
\dot y+\delta y
and w(0)=y(0), the comparison principle yields
w(t)\ge y(t).
∎

Corollary 2.15 — Threshold persistence
Let w_c>0 be a required persistence threshold. If
w_{\mathrm{eq}}>w_c
and
w(0)\ge w_c,
then
w(t)\ge w_c
for all t\ge0.

 Proof
The lower comparison solution is a convex combination of
w(0) and w_{\mathrm{eq}}:
y(t)
=
e^{-\delta t}w(0)
+
(1-e^{-\delta t})w_{\mathrm{eq}}.
Both terms are at least w_c, so y(t)\ge w_c. Since w(t)\ge
y(t), the result follows. ∎
This gives a precise sufficient condition for persistence
above a threshold.

2.17 Interaction Quality Model
Consider
\dot w_{ij}
=
q_{ij}\chi_{ij}I_{ij}
\delta_{ij}w_{ij}
+
\eta_{ij},
with

 q_{ij}\in[-1,1],
\qquad
\chi_{ij}\ge0,
\qquad
I_{ij}\ge0,
\qquad
\delta_{ij}>0.
Assume these quantities are constant and \eta_{ij}=0.

Proposition 2.16 — Exact coupling trajectory
w_{ij}(t)
=
w_{ij}^*
+
\left(
w_{ij}(0)-w_{ij}^*
\right)e^{-\delta_{ij}t},
where
w_{ij}^*
=
\frac{q_{ij}\chi_{ij}I_{ij}}{\delta_{ij}}.

Proof
This is a linear first-order differential equation:
\dot w+\delta w=q\chi I.

 Solving by the integrating-factor method gives the stated
formula. ∎

Corollary 2.17 — Sign of long-term coupling
If
\chi_{ij}I_{ij}>0,
then the sign of the equilibrium coupling equals the sign of
q_{ij}.
Thus constructive and destructive interactions can be
formally distinguished by the sign of the quality factor in this
simplified model.

2.18 Feedback as Retained-State
Dependence
A system possesses feedback when future transitions depend
on a consequence of previous transitions.
Let
m_{n+1}=G(m_n,A_n)
and
A_{n+1}=H(x_{n+1},m_{n+1}).

 Theorem 2.18 — Minimal feedback criterion
If there exist m,\tilde m and an active state x such that
H(x,m)\neq H(x,\tilde m),
then retained state participates in the generation of future
interaction.

Proof
The same active state x produces different future interactions
when paired with different retained states. Therefore the
retained state is causally represented in the transition rule of
the model. ∎
This is a formal criterion inside the model. Empirical
causality requires additional experimental identification.

2.19 Feedback Isomorphism
Let two closed recursive systems be
S_1=(\Omega_1,T_1,K_1,C_1)
and
S_2=(\Omega_2,T_2,K_2,C_2).
Suppose there exists a bijection
\phi:\Omega_1\rightarrow\Omega_2

 such that
\phi\circ T_1=T_2\circ\phi
and a constraint-space bijection
\psi:K_1\rightarrow K_2
such that
C_2\circ\phi=\psi\circ C_1.

Theorem 2.19 — Trajectory conjugacy
For every n\ge0,
\phi\circ T_1^n
=
T_2^n\circ\phi.

Proof
Proceed by induction.
For n=0,
\phi\circ I=I\circ\phi.
Assume
\phi\circ T_1^n
=
T_2^n\circ\phi.
Then

 \begin{aligned}
\phi\circ T_1^{n+1}
&=
\phi\circ T_1\circ T_1^n\\
&=
T_2\circ\phi\circ T_1^n\\
&=
T_2\circ T_2^n\circ\phi\\
&=
T_2^{n+1}\circ\phi.
\end{aligned}
Therefore the result holds for all n. ∎

Corollary 2.20 — Constraint preservation
along trajectories
For every initial state x\in\Omega_1,
C_2\bigl(T_2^n(\phi(x))\bigr)
=
\psi\left(
C_1(T_1^n(x))
\right).

Proof
Using trajectory conjugacy,

 T_2^n(\phi(x))
=
\phi(T_1^n(x)).
Then
C_2(T_2^n(\phi(x)))
=
C_2(\phi(T_1^n(x)))
=
\psi(C_1(T_1^n(x))).
∎
This proves preservation of abstract recursive architecture
under conjugacy. It does not establish material or physical
identity.

2.20 Organizational Identity as an
Equivalence Class
Let
\mathcal Q:\mathcal Z\rightarrow\mathcal Y
extract the organizational features regarded as identityrelevant.
Define
z\sim_{\mathcal Q}\tilde z

 if
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(\tilde z).

Lemma 2.21 — Identity relation
The relation \sim_{\mathcal Q} is an equivalence relation.

Proof
Reflexivity:
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(z),
so z\sim_{\mathcal Q}z.
Symmetry: If
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(\tilde z),
then
\mathcal Q(\tilde z)=\mathcal Q(z).
Transitivity: If
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(\tilde z)
and
\mathcal Q(\tilde z)=\mathcal Q(\hat z),
then
\mathcal Q(z)=\mathcal Q(\hat z).

 Thus \sim_{\mathcal Q} is an equivalence relation. ∎
The identity of the modeled system is then represented by the
equivalence class
[z]_{\mathcal Q}.

2.21 Identity Preservation Under
Dynamics
Definition 2.5 — Exact organizational
identity preservation
A transition T preserves organizational identity if
\mathcal Q(T(z))=\mathcal Q(z)
for every admissible state z.

Theorem 2.22 — Orbit identity preservation
If T preserves \mathcal Q, then
\mathcal Q(T^n(z))=\mathcal Q(z)
for all n\ge0.

Proof
Induction gives

 \mathcal Q(T^{n+1}(z))
=
\mathcal Q(T(T^n(z)))
=
\mathcal Q(T^n(z)).
Beginning with \mathcal Q(T(z))=\mathcal Q(z), repeated
application yields the result. ∎

2.22 Approximate Identity
Preservation
Exact invariance is often too strong.
Let d_{\mathcal Y} be a metric on organizational feature
space.
Define identity drift over one step by
\Delta_{\mathcal Q}(z)
=
d_{\mathcal Y}
\left(
\mathcal Q(T(z)),
\mathcal Q(z)
\right).
If
\Delta_{\mathcal Q}(z)\le\varepsilon,

 identity is preserved within tolerance \varepsilon for that
step.

Proposition 2.23 — Cumulative drift bound
Suppose
d_{\mathcal Y}
\left(
\mathcal Q(z_{k+1}),
\mathcal Q(z_k)
\right)
\le
\varepsilon_k.
Then
d_{\mathcal Y}
\left(
\mathcal Q(z_n),
\mathcal Q(z_0)
\right)
\le
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_k.

Proof
Apply the triangle inequality repeatedly:
\begin{aligned}
d(\mathcal Q(z_n),\mathcal Q(z_0))

 &\le
d(\mathcal Q(z_n),\mathcal Q(z_{n-1}))\\
&\quad+
d(\mathcal Q(z_{n-1}),\mathcal Q(z_{n-2}))
+\cdots\\
&\quad+
d(\mathcal Q(z_1),\mathcal Q(z_0))\\
&\le
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_k.
\end{aligned}
∎
Small local drift does not necessarily imply indefinite
identity preservation unless the accumulated drift remains
bounded.

2.23 Progress as Possibility
Improvement
A possibility space needs an ordering before “improvement”
can be formalized.
Let
V:\mathcal P(\Omega)\rightarrow\mathbb R
be a viability or opportunity functional.
Define progress by

 V(\mathcal P_{n+1})>V(\mathcal P_n).

Definition 2.6 — Retention-mediated
progress
An interaction produces retention-mediated progress if
m_{n+1}=G(m_n,A_n)
and
V(\Pi_1(x_{n+1},m_{n+1}))
>
V(\Pi_1(x_n,m_n)).
This definition makes explicit that “expanded possibility”
depends on a chosen and justified functional V.

Proposition 2.24 — Progress is not equivalent
to set enlargement
It is possible for
\mathcal P_{n+1}\not\supseteq\mathcal P_n
while
V(\mathcal P_{n+1})>V(\mathcal P_n).

Proof by example
Let

 \mathcal P_n=\{1,100\}
and
\mathcal P_{n+1}=\{50,60\}.
Neither set contains the other.
Define
V(\mathcal P)
=
\min_{x\in\mathcal P}x.
Then
V(\mathcal P_n)=1,
\qquad
V(\mathcal P_{n+1})=50.
Thus opportunity can improve according to a selected
criterion without simple set inclusion. ∎
Therefore progress always requires a value structure, not
merely a larger number of reachable states.

2.24 Communication as Coupled
Memory Update
Let two systems have states

 z_1=(x_1,m_1),
\qquad
z_2=(x_2,m_2).
A communication event is represented by
\mathcal C_{12}:
(z_1,z_2)
\mapsto
(z_1',z_2').
Communication changes receiver memory if
m_2'\neq m_2.
It changes receiver possibility if
\Pi_1^x(x_2',m_2')
\neq
\Pi_1^x(x_2,m_2).

Theorem 2.25 — Communication-topossibility criterion
Suppose the communication event changes receiver memory
from m_2 to m_2', while the receiver active state remains
x_2. If
F(x_2,m_2,u)
\neq
F(x_2,m_2',u)

 for some admissible input u, then communication has
changed at least one future receiver transition.

Proof
Before communication, input u produces
F(x_2,m_2,u).
After communication, the same input produces
F(x_2,m_2',u).
By assumption these differ, so the receiver’s future inputstate relation has changed. ∎

2.25 Response as Transformation
Let memory be transformed by
\Delta:\mathcal M\rightarrow\mathcal M'.
The future possibility set becomes
\Pi_1(x,\Delta(m)).
A response is future-expanding relative to functional V if
V\bigl(\Pi_1(x,\Delta(m))\bigr)
>
V\bigl(\Pi_1(x,m)\bigr).
A response is future-contracting if the inequality is reversed.

 A response may also preserve value while reorganizing
possibilities.

2.26 Master Recursive Chain
The complete formal chain is
z_n=(x_n,m_n),
\mathcal P_n=\Pi_1(z_n),
u_n=\Sigma(z_n),
A_n=T(z_n,u_n),
m_{n+1}=G(z_n,u_n),
x_{n+1}=F(z_n,u_n),
\mathcal P_{n+1}=\Pi_1(x_{n+1},m_{n+1}).
Compressed:
\boxed{
\mathcal P_n
\rightarrow
\Sigma_n
\rightarrow
A_n
\rightarrow
M_{n+1}
\rightarrow

 \mathcal P_{n+1}
}
This is not an additional physical law. It is a formal
decomposition of recursive systems possessing statedependent possibility, realized transition, retained update,
and future influence.

2.27 Central Theorem of Retained
Consequence
Theorem 2.26 — Retained consequence

Let

The theorem is logically simple because the scientific burden
lies in identifying and validating the state variables,

2.28 Minimal Defensible Theorem
Theorem 2.27 — Recursive organization
theorem
Assume:
1. the system has an augmented state z_n=(x_n,m_n);
2. the retained state is updated recursively;
3. future transition structure depends nontrivially on m_n;
4. trajectories remain inside an admissible domain.
Then prior interactions can influence later reachable states
through the retained-state channel.

Proof
By assumption 2, prior interaction contributes to m_n.
By assumption 3, there exist retained states producing
different future transition structures at some active state.

 Therefore the retained consequence generated by prior
interaction can alter a later successor or reachable set.
Assumption 4 ensures the recursion remains within the stated
model domain. ∎
This is the rigorous form of the statement:
What happens can change what can happen next.
It is conditional, not universal. It applies precisely to models
satisfying the assumptions.

2.29 No-Go Results
Theorem 2.28 — No retained influence
without sensitivity
If
F(x,m,u)=F(x,\tilde m,u)
for all states, retained values, and admissible inputs, and if
admissibility is also independent of memory, then retained
consequence cannot change active-state possibility.

Proof
The successor map and admissible-input set are identical for
every retained state. Therefore all projected possibility sets
are identical. ∎

 Theorem 2.29 — No feedback without
retained dependence
If future transition rules are independent of every variable
altered by previous interaction, then the model contains no
feedback channel from past consequence to future evolution.

Proof
Feedback requires a path by which an earlier consequence
enters a later transition. If every later transition is
independent of all earlier altered variables, no such path
exists. ∎

Theorem 2.30 — Persistence does not imply
value
A persistent state can preserve a negative, harmful, unstable,
or low-viability structure.

Proof by construction
Consider
m_{n+1}=m_n
with
m_0=-1.
Then

 m_n=-1
for all n, so the state persists perfectly.
Define value
V(m)=m.
Then the persistent state has negative value. Hence
persistence alone implies neither benefit nor progress. ∎

The formal results above establish:
• how retained state may be encoded;
• how it may alter future transitions or reachable sets;
• how finite-history systems admit augmented-state
closure;
• how persistence thresholds arise in simple dynamical
models;
• how feedback isomorphism preserves recursive
structure;
• how identity can be represented through invariant
organizational features;
• how communication and response may change future
possibility;
• why progress requires a separate value functional.
They do not establish:
• that every real system is accurately modeled this way;

that persistence is universally beneficial;
that structural similarity implies physical identity;
that consciousness or conscious intent follows from

evidence.

3.31 Rank, Redundancy, Tightness,
and Uniqueness
These four concepts must be separated.

Definition 3.4 — Rank completeness
\operatorname{rank}(PR)=8.

Definition 3.5 — Redundancy
There are more centered channel vectors than the minimum
number required to span \mathbb R^8.

Definition 3.6 — Tightness
R^TPR=\alpha I_8.

Definition 3.7 — Uniqueness

 No admissible alternative channel architecture satisfies the
specified mathematical and physical criteria.

Theorem 3.37 — Logical independence
Rank completeness, redundancy, tightness, and uniqueness
are not equivalent.

Proof
• A basis of eight vectors can have full rank without
redundancy.
• A redundant family can still fail full rank if all vectors
lie in a lower-dimensional subspace.
• A full-rank frame need not be tight.
• A tight frame need not be unique; many inequivalent
tight frames exist.
• Uniqueness requires a classification or extremal theorem
beyond rank and frame conditions.
Thus no one property implies all the others. ∎

A braid word remains in the same braid-group element

4.40 Existence by the Direct

Let \mathcal A_Q be an admissible set in fixed

existence
Suppose:
1. \mathcal A_Q is nonempty;
2. E is bounded below on \mathcal A_Q;
3. every minimizing sequence has a weakly convergent
subsequence;
4. \mathcal A_Q is weakly closed;
5. E is weakly lower semicontinuous.

\le
\liminf E[\Psi_n]

\inf_{\mathcal A_Q}E.
Therefore equality holds and \Psi_* is a minimizer. ∎

7.1 The Completed Zeta Function
For complex s, define the completed Riemann zeta function
\xi(s)
=
\frac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}
\Gamma\!\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\zeta(s).
This normalization removes the pole of \zeta(s) at s=1,
incorporates the trivial zeros, and produces an entire
function.
The completed function satisfies the functional equation

 \boxed{\xi(s)=\xi(1-s)}.
It also respects complex conjugation,
\boxed{\xi(\overline s)=\overline{\xi(s)}}.
Combining both gives
\boxed{
\xi(s)
=
\overline{\xi(1-\overline s)}
}.

7.2 Entirety of \xi
Theorem 7.1 — The completed function is
entire
The apparent singularities in
\xi(s)
=
\frac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}
\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)
are removable, and \xi extends to an entire function on
\mathbb C.

Proof outline

 The zeta function has a simple pole at s=1, canceled by the
factor s-1.
The gamma factor has poles at the nonpositive even integers,
s=0,-2,-4,\ldots,
but the trivial zeros of \zeta(s) cancel those poles for negative
even s. The remaining apparent singularity at s=0 is canceled
by the factor s, together with the functional-equation
structure.
After these cancellations, the product has no poles and
extends holomorphically throughout the plane. ∎
A full analytic proof normally proceeds through the thetafunction representation or analytic continuation of \zeta.

7.3 Symmetry Axes
The map
s\mapsto1-s
is reflection across the vertical line
\operatorname{Re}s=\frac12
followed by complex conjugation only when expressed
geometrically in the plane.
The map

 s\mapsto1-\overline s
is the direct mirror reflection across the critical line.
Indeed, for
s=\sigma+it,
1-\overline s
=
1-\sigma+it.
The imaginary coordinate remains t, while \sigma reflects to
1-\sigma.

7.4 Critical Line
The fixed points of the mirror map satisfy
s=1-\overline s.
Writing s=\sigma+it,
\sigma+it
=
1-\sigma+it.
Therefore
2\sigma=1,
so
\boxed{\sigma=\frac12}.

 Thus the critical line is precisely the fixed-point set of the
symmetry
s\mapsto1-\overline s.

7.5 The Symmetry Defect Operator
Define
D(s)
=
\xi(s)
\overline{\xi(1-\overline s)}.
One may then define the nonnegative defect energy
E_D(s)
=
|D(s)|^2.
At first glance, one might hope that minimizing E_D forces s
onto the critical line.
That hope fails for a decisive reason.

Theorem 7.2 — The proposed defect vanishes
identically
For every

 s\in\mathbb C,
D(s)=0.
Consequently,
E_D(s)=0
for every s.

Proof
By complex conjugation symmetry,
\overline{\xi(1-\overline s)}
=
\xi(1-s).
By the functional equation,
\xi(1-s)=\xi(s).
Therefore
D(s)
=
\xi(s)-\xi(s)
=
0.
Hence
E_D(s)=|0|^2=0.
∎

 7.6 Consequence for Critical-Line
Arguments
Corollary 7.3 — No localization information
The condition
D(s)=0
does not imply
\operatorname{Re}s=\frac12.

Proof
The defect vanishes for every point in the complex plane,
including points off the critical line. Therefore its zero set is
all of \mathbb C, not only the critical line. ∎
This is the central non-circularity test.
A quantity derived solely from an identity already known to
hold everywhere cannot distinguish the critical line from offline points.

\quad\Longrightarrow\quad

Let
\rho=\beta+i\gamma
be a nonreal nontrivial zero.
Then the following are also zeros:
\overline\rho=\beta-i\gamma,
1-\rho=1-\beta-i\gamma,
1-\overline\rho=1-\beta+i\gamma.

=
\overline{\xi(\rho)}
=
0.
The functional equation gives

If \beta\neq1/2 and \gamma\neq0, none of the reflection or
conjugation operations fixes \rho, so all four are distinct. ∎

If
\beta=\frac12,
then
1-\overline\rho=\rho,
and the quartet collapses to the conjugate pair
\frac12\pm i\gamma.
The hypothesis asserts that every nonreal nontrivial zero
exhibits this collapse.

Proof
The polynomial construction supplies a counterexample to
the general logical implication. ∎
Therefore any proof must use more than the known
functional symmetry.

 7.12 A Genuine SymmetryLocalization Quantity
A quantity that detects distance from the critical line is
\delta(s)
=
s-(1-\overline s).
For
s=\sigma+it,
\delta(s)
=
2\sigma-1.
Hence
|\delta(s)|^2
=
(2\sigma-1)^2.
This vanishes exactly on the critical line.
But this observation is purely geometric.
It says nothing about whether zeros of \xi must satisfy
\delta(\rho)=0.

 7.13 Weighted Zero Localization
Functional
One can define
J(s)
=
|\xi(s)|^2
+
\lambda
\left(
\operatorname{Re}s-\frac12
\right)^2,
\qquad
\lambda>0.
This has a penalty favoring the critical line.
However, such a functional does not prove that off-line zeros
cannot exist.
At an off-line zero \rho,
J(\rho)
=
\lambda
\left(
\beta-\frac12
\right)^2
>0,

 while a nonzero critical-line point may have larger or smaller
value depending on |\xi|.
The penalty was inserted by definition; it was not derived
from a theorem forcing the zero set.

7.14 Nonnegative Energy
Functionals
A common strategy is to construct
\mathcal J[\xi]
\ge0
and attempt to show its minimum occurs precisely when all
zeros lie on the critical line.
For this to prove the hypothesis, at least three properties are
needed.

Required properties
1. Exact zero-set equivalence
\mathcal J=0
\iff
\text{all nontrivial zeros lie on }\operatorname{Re}
s=\frac12.
2. Independent nonnegativity proof
\mathcal J\ge0
without assuming the hypothesis.

 3. Well-defined convergence
All sums, products, and integrals used to define \mathcal
J must converge or be rigorously regularized.
A functional lacking any one of these is not yet an equivalent
criterion.

7.15 Trivial Nonnegative
Functionals
For example,
\mathcal J_0
=
\sum_\rho
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2w(\rho),
with positive weights w(\rho), would satisfy
\mathcal J_0=0
if and only if all zeros lie on the critical line—assuming the
sum converges and includes all zeros.
But evaluating or proving vanishing of this functional is
exactly as hard as proving the hypothesis. It merely restates
the claim.

 Proposition 7.9 — Equivalent reformulation
is not automatically progress
Writing the Riemann Hypothesis as the vanishing of a
nonnegative sum does not prove it unless the vanishing is
established independently.

Proof
The equivalence changes notation but not logical difficulty. ∎

7.16 Hadamard Product
The completed function is an entire function of order one and
admits a canonical product representation. In an appropriate
normalization,
\xi(s)
=
\xi(0)
\prod_\rho
\left(
1-\frac{s}{\rho}
\right)
when zeros are paired or the product is interpreted in its
canonical form.
More carefully, a genus-one product may be written with
exponential factors,

 \xi(s)
=
e^{A+Bs}
\prod_\rho
\left(
1-\frac{s}{\rho}
\right)
e^{s/\rho}.
The exact presentation depends on how symmetric pairing is
handled.

7.17 Logarithmic Derivative
Away from zeros,
\frac{\xi'(s)}{\xi(s)}
can be expressed as a sum over zeros.
Formally,
\frac{\xi'(s)}{\xi(s)}
=
B
+
\sum_\rho
\left(
\frac{1}{s-\rho}
+

 \frac{1}{\rho}
\right).
With symmetric regularization, simplified versions are
available.
This identity connects the analytic behavior of \xi to the
geometry of its zero set.

7.18 Logarithmic Potential
Define
U(s)
=
-\log|\xi(s)|
away from zeros.
Near a simple zero \rho,
\xi(s)
=
\xi'(\rho)(s-\rho)
+
O((s-\rho)^2),
so
U(s)
=
-\log|s-\rho|

 -\log|\xi'(\rho)|
+
o(1).
Thus zeros behave like logarithmic singularities of the
potential.

7.19 Laplacian of the Logarithmic
Potential
In two real dimensions, the distributional identity
\Delta\log|s-\rho|
=
2\pi\delta_\rho
holds.
Therefore, formally,
\Delta\log|\xi(s)|
=
2\pi
\sum_\rho
m_\rho\delta_\rho
away from contributions of nonzero analytic prefactors.
Here m_\rho is the zero multiplicity.
This identifies the zeros as point sources in logarithmicpotential language.

 It does not constrain those sources to the critical line.

7.20 Functional Symmetry of the
Potential
Because
|\xi(s)|
=
|\xi(1-\overline s)|,
the potential satisfies
U(s)
=
U(1-\overline s).
Therefore U is mirror symmetric about the critical line.
Again, mirror symmetry permits paired off-line singularities.

7.21 Transverse Coordinate
Write
s
=
\frac12+x+it,
where x measures horizontal displacement from the critical
line.

 The functional symmetry gives
\xi\!\left(\frac12+x+it\right)
=
\overline{
\xi\!\left(\frac12-x+it\right)
}.
Therefore
\left|
\xi\!\left(\frac12+x+it\right)
\right|
=
\left|
\xi\!\left(\frac12-x+it\right)
\right|.
Thus
U(x,t)=U(-x,t).

7.22 First Transverse Derivative
If U is differentiable at x=0, then evenness implies
\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}(0,t)=0.

Proposition 7.10 — Critical line is a
stationary symmetry line
At points where \xi(1/2+it)\neq0, the transverse derivative of

 \log|\xi|
vanishes on the critical line.

Proof
An even differentiable function has zero first derivative at
the origin. ∎
This stationarity is automatic from symmetry and does not
indicate that the line is a minimum.

7.23 Transverse Second Derivative
For a nonvanishing analytic function f, \log|f| is harmonic:
\Delta\log|f|=0.
With coordinates x,t,
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\log|\xi|
+
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}\log|\xi|
=
0
away from zeros.
Therefore on the critical line,
\partial_x^2\log|\xi|
=
-\partial_t^2\log|\xi|.

 The sign of the transverse curvature is not fixed globally.

Proposition 7.11 — Symmetry does not imply
transverse minimality
An even function can have a minimum, maximum, or higherorder saddle at the origin.

Proof by examples
f(x)=x^2
has a minimum,
f(x)=-x^2
has a maximum,
and
f(x)=x^4
has a flat minimum.
All are even. ∎
Thus a zero transverse first derivative on the critical line
proves no confinement.

7.24 Transverse Hessian of |\xi|^2
Define

 F(x,t)
=
\left|
\xi\!\left(\frac12+x+it\right)
\right|^2.
Then
F(x,t)=F(-x,t).
At x=0,
F_x=0.
The second derivative is
F_{xx}
=
2|\xi_x|^2
+
2\operatorname{Re}
\left(
\overline\xi\,\xi_{xx}
\right).
At a critical-line zero \rho=1/2+i\gamma, where \xi(\rho)=0,
F_{xx}(0,\gamma)
=
2|\xi'(\rho)|^2
for a simple zero, after identifying \partial_x with complex
differentiation along the real direction.

 Hence a simple critical-line zero is locally quadratic in the
transverse direction.

7.25 Local Shape Near a Simple
Zero
Let \rho be a simple zero.
Then
\xi(s)
=
\xi'(\rho)(s-\rho)
+
O(|s-\rho|^2).
Therefore
|\xi(s)|^2
=
|\xi'(\rho)|^2|s-\rho|^2
+
O(|s-\rho|^3).

Theorem 7.12 — Local isotropic leading
order
To leading order, the squared modulus near a simple zero is
radially symmetric in the complex plane.

 Proof
The leading term depends only on
|s-\rho|^2.
∎
Therefore local Hessian positivity of |\xi|^2 at a zero does not
distinguish whether the zero is on or off the critical line.
Every simple zero is locally a strict minimum of |\xi|^2.

7.26 Failure of Local-Minimum
Arguments
Corollary 7.13
The fact that
|\xi(s)|^2\ge0
and vanishes at a zero does not favor critical-line zeros over
off-line zeros.

Proof
Every zero, wherever located, is a global minimum of the
nonnegative function |\xi|^2, with minimum value zero. ∎
A local or global minimization of |\xi|^2 finds zeros, not their
required real part.

 7.27 Symmetric Off-Line Pair
Potential
Suppose an off-line pair at fixed height is
\rho_\pm
=
\frac12\pm a+i\gamma,
\qquad
a>0.
Consider the factor
P(s)
=
(s-\rho_+)(s-\rho_-).
On the horizontal line t=\gamma, write
s=\frac12+x+i\gamma.
Then
P(s)
=
(x-a)(x+a)
=
x^2-a^2.
Therefore

 |P(s)|^2
=
(x^2-a^2)^2.
At the symmetry axis x=0,
|P|^2=a^4,
while the zeros occur at x=\pm a.

Proposition 7.14 — A symmetric off-line pair
can make the critical line a local maximum
For
f(x)=(x^2-a^2)^2,
f''(0)=-4a^2<0.

Proof
f'(x)=4x(x^2-a^2),
f''(x)=12x^2-4a^2.
At x=0, the result follows. ∎
Thus symmetric off-line zeros naturally produce a ridge, not
a valley, on the critical line at the same height.
This illustrates why transverse curvature information could
be relevant—but proving a global sign condition strong
enough to exclude every off-line pair is the hard part.

 7.28 Quartet Factor
For an off-line quartet,
\rho=\frac12+a+i\gamma,
1-\overline\rho=\frac12-a+i\gamma,
and their conjugates, define
Q(s)
=
\prod_{\omega\in\{\rho,1-\overline\rho,\overline\rho,1\rho\}}
(s-\omega).
On the critical line,
s=\frac12+it.
Then the quartet contribution is real and nonnegative after
suitable pairing:
Q\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\left[
a^2+(t-\gamma)^2
\right]
\left[
a^2+(t+\gamma)^2
\right].

 This factor does not vanish for real t when a\neq0.
An off-line quartet therefore modifies the magnitude of \xi
on the critical line without creating a critical-line zero at the
same height.

7.29 Can Off-Line Quartets Cancel?
Products do not “cancel” zeros in the ordinary sense.
If \rho is a zero of an entire function, multiplying by other
nonzero factors does not remove it.
Only a pole at the same point could cancel a zero, but \xi is
entire and its canonical product has no such poles.

Theorem 7.15 — Distinct zeros cannot cancel
in an entire product
A zero at \rho remains a zero regardless of the presence of
other zeros at symmetric locations.

Proof
Factor locally:
\xi(s)
=
(s-\rho)^m g(s),
where g(\rho)\neq0.

 Other distinct zeros contribute factors nonzero at \rho.
Therefore the multiplicity m remains. ∎
The phrase “phase cancellation between symmetric zero
pairs” must not be used as though zeros could annihilate one
another algebraically.

7.30 Cancellation of Contributions
to Derived Quantities
Symmetric zeros can cancel in certain sums.
For example, terms odd under
\rho\mapsto1-\overline\rho
may cancel when summed over a symmetric quartet.
But cancellation in a derived statistic does not remove the
zeros themselves.
A valid proof must identify the exact statistic, prove
convergence, and show why vanishing of that statistic
excludes—not merely hides—off-line zeros.

7.31 A Symmetric Sum That Always
Vanishes
Consider

 S
=
\sum_\rho
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)
w(\rho),
with weights symmetric under reflection:
w(\rho)=w(1-\overline\rho).
Each off-line pair contributes
a\,w+(-a)\,w=0.

Proposition 7.16 — Vanishing first moment
does not imply the hypothesis
A symmetric zero set automatically has zero centered first
moment, even if off-line zeros exist.

Proof
Reflection pairs cancel term by term. ∎
A useful criterion must involve an even, nonnegative
measure such as squared displacement, not a signed first
moment.

7.32 Second Moment

 Define formally
M_2
=
\sum_\rho
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2w(\rho),
\qquad
w(\rho)>0.
Then every term is nonnegative.
If the sum converges and includes every nontrivial zero,
M_2=0
if and only if the Riemann Hypothesis holds.

Theorem 7.17 — Weighted-square
equivalence
Under convergence and strictly positive weights,
M_2=0
\iff
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12
for every included zero.

Proof

 A sum of nonnegative terms is zero if and only if every term
is zero. ∎
This is a valid equivalent formulation, but proving M_2=0
remains the full problem.

7.33 Truncated Numerical Second
Moment
Let
M_2(T)
=
\sum_{|\operatorname{Im}\rho|\le T}
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2.
If all numerically verified zeros up to height T lie on the
critical line, then
M_2(T)=0
within numerical precision.
This establishes only a finite-height verification.
It says nothing directly about zeros above T.

7.34 Finite Verification Boundary

 Proposition 7.18 — No finite computation
proves the universal claim
Verifying that the first N zeros lie on the critical line does not
prove that every zero does.

Proof
A universal statement over an infinite set cannot be deduced
solely from finitely many checked instances without an
additional theorem reducing the infinite case to those
instances. ∎
Numerical verification is valuable evidence and a
consistency check, but not a complete proof.

7.35 Argument Principle
For a meromorphic function f with no zeros or poles on a
closed contour C,
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\oint_C
\frac{f'(s)}{f(s)}\,ds
=
N_Z-N_P,
where zeros and poles are counted with multiplicity inside C.
For \xi, which is entire,

 \frac{1}{2\pi i}
\oint_C
\frac{\xi'(s)}{\xi(s)}\,ds
=
N_Z.
This allows rigorous zero counting in finite regions if the
contour integral is controlled.

7.36 Zero Counting Does Not
Localize Horizontally
The argument principle counts total zeros inside a region.
To prove the hypothesis, one must compare:
• the number of zeros in the full critical strip up to height
T;
• the number of zeros found on the critical line up to
height T.
If these counts agree for all T, the hypothesis follows.
Finite verification proves equality only up to a finite height.

7.37 Hardy’s Z-Function
Define
Z(t)
=

 e^{i\vartheta(t)}
\zeta\!\left(\frac12+it\right),
with \vartheta(t) chosen so that Z(t) is real for real t.
Zeros of Z(t) correspond to zeros of \zeta on the critical line.
Sign changes of Z(t) locate odd-multiplicity critical-line
zeros.
This is a genuine line-restricted tool, unlike the identically
vanishing symmetry defect.

7.38 Limitation of the Z-Function
Finding many zeros of Z(t) proves many critical-line zeros
exist.
It does not exclude additional off-line zeros unless combined
with a total zero count.
Therefore a complete finite-height verification requires both:
1. locating all critical-line zeros up to T;
2. proving the total number of strip zeros up to T is the
same.

7.39 Riemann–von Mangoldt
Counting Formula

 The number N(T) of nontrivial zeros with imaginary part
between 0 and T, counted with multiplicity, satisfies
N(T)
=
\frac{T}{2\pi}
\log\left(\frac{T}{2\pi}\right)
\frac{T}{2\pi}
+
O(\log T).
More precise versions include an argument term involving
\zeta.
This formula counts zeros but does not prove their real parts.

7.40 Equivalent Criteria
The Riemann Hypothesis has many genuine equivalent
formulations.
Examples include statements involving:
•
•
•
•
•
•

bounds on summatory arithmetic functions;
positivity conditions;
zero-free regions;
the Li coefficients;
spectral interpretations, if fully established;
growth bounds for \zeta or related functions.

 An equivalent criterion is useful only when its truth can be
established by methods not already assuming the hypothesis.

7.41 Li’s Criterion
Define Li coefficients by
\lambda_n
=
\frac{1}{(n-1)!}
\left.
\frac{d^n}{ds^n}
\left[
s^{n-1}\log\xi(s)
\right]
\right|_{s=1}.
Li’s criterion states that the Riemann Hypothesis is
equivalent to
\lambda_n>0
for every positive integer n.
This is a true positivity reformulation.
Yet proving infinitely many inequalities remains difficult.

7.42 Why Li-Type Positivity Is
Different

 The symmetry defect
D(s)
vanishes because of an identity valid everywhere.
Li coefficients instead encode the entire zero distribution
through derivatives of \log\xi.
Their positivity is not already guaranteed by the functional
equation.
Therefore they carry genuine additional content.

7.43 Hilbert–Pólya Direction
A spectral proof would seek a self-adjoint operator H whose
eigenvalues correspond to the imaginary parts of nontrivial
zeros:
H\psi_n=\gamma_n\psi_n,
with zeros
\rho_n=\frac12+i\gamma_n.
Self-adjointness would force \gamma_n\in\mathbb R.
However, to prove the hypothesis one must construct the
operator and establish exact spectral correspondence.
A merely suggestive Hamiltonian or numerical similarity is
insufficient.

 7.44 Necessary Burden for a
Spectral Proof
A valid Hilbert–Pólya-style proof requires:
1. a precisely defined Hilbert space;
2. a densely defined operator;
3. proof of self-adjointness or an appropriate equivalent;
4. proof of discrete or controlled spectrum;
5. exact identification of the spectral determinant or
counting function with \xi;
6. multiplicity correspondence;
7. exclusion of extra eigenvalues and missing zeros.
Without these, the construction remains a conjectural
analogy.

7.45 A Transverse Coherence
Hamiltonian
Suppose one defines an operator
H_\perp
=
-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}
+
V(x,t)
in the transverse coordinate x=\sigma-1/2.

 To infer the Riemann Hypothesis, one would need to prove
that zero states of the relevant spectral problem occur only at
x=0.
This requires a theorem linking eigenfunctions or
eigenvalues of H_\perp exactly to zeros of \xi.
A potential built from |\xi| may encode the zeros, but unless
the spectral equivalence is rigorous, the construction is only
a repackaging.

7.46 Circular Potential Construction
For example, defining
V(s)
=
|\xi(s)|^2
and observing that minima occur at zeros is circular if the
goal is to derive the zero locations.
The potential was built using the very function whose zeros
are being investigated.
This may be useful for visualization or numerical search, but
not automatically for proof.

 7.47 Symmetric Off-Line Pair
Contradiction: Required Form
A valid contradiction argument would need to assume an offline zero
\rho=\frac12+a+i\gamma,
\qquad
a\neq0,
derive the full quartet, and then prove that the quartet
violates an independently established theorem.
Possible contradiction targets might include:
• positivity of a rigorously derived quadratic form;
• a zero-counting identity;
• a spectral self-adjointness theorem;
• a growth bound;
• an arithmetic explicit formula.
Symmetry alone supplies the quartet but no contradiction.

7.48 Why “No Phase Cancellation”
Is Insufficient
Suppose a proposed functional contains contributions
J(\rho)+J(1-\overline\rho).
To claim they cannot cancel, one must prove:

 1. the contributions are well defined;
2. their signs are controlled;
3. the infinite sum converges;
4. no other zeros contribute compensating terms;
5. the resulting nonzero quantity contradicts a known
identity.
Merely asserting that symmetric pairs cannot cancel does not
establish any of these.

7.49 Positive Pair Contribution
A promising form is an even pair functional,
Q(\rho)
=
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2w(\rho),
\qquad
w(\rho)>0.
Then the mirror pair contributes
2a^2w(\rho)
when the weights are symmetric.
This cannot cancel within the pair.
But one still must prove the sum of all such positive
contributions is zero from independent mathematics.

 That final step is equivalent to proving the hypothesis.

7.50 Explicit-Formula Route
The zeros enter explicit formulas connecting prime-counting
quantities to sums over \rho.
A proof might derive a bound on an arithmetic error term
strong enough to imply
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12.
This route uses arithmetic information beyond the functional
equation.
Any residual-coherence interpretation would need to
reproduce such a rigorous bound, not merely visualize
symmetry.

7.51 Non-Circularity Checklist
For every proposed proof ingredient, ask:
1. Does this identity already follow from the functional
equation?
2. Does it vanish or hold everywhere, not only at zeros?
3. Was the critical-line penalty inserted by definition?
4. Does the argument assume all zeros can be paired in the
desired way?

 5. Does it exchange an infinite proof for finite numerical
evidence?
6. Does it use \xi to construct a potential whose minima are
then said to explain \xi’s zeros?
7. Is the key positivity independent of the hypothesis?
8. Are convergence and regularization justified?
9. Is every zero included with multiplicity?
10.Does the conclusion exclude off-line quartets rather than
merely respect their symmetry?
A failure on any central item leaves the proof incomplete.

7.52 A Corrected Defect Concept
One may define a geometric displacement defect for a zero
\rho,
\Delta_\rho
=
\rho-(1-\overline\rho)
=
2
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right).
Then
|\Delta_\rho|^2
=
4

 \left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2.
A global defect could be
\mathcal D
=
\sum_\rho
w(\rho)|\Delta_\rho|^2.
Under suitable positive weights and convergence,
\mathcal D=0
is equivalent to the hypothesis.
This is mathematically honest—but it is a reformulation, not
yet a proof.

7.53 Central No-Go Theorem
Theorem 7.19 — Functional-equation defect
no-go
Let F be any function satisfying
F(s)
=
\overline{F(1-\overline s)}
for all s.

 Define
D_F(s)
=
F(s)
\overline{F(1-\overline s)}.
Then
D_F\equiv0.
Therefore no conclusion about the location of zeros of F can
be obtained from the condition
D_F(s)=0.

Proof
The defining symmetry gives the identity immediately. Since
the condition is satisfied at every point, it cannot distinguish
zeros or fixed points of the symmetry. ∎
This theorem applies directly to the completed zeta function.

7.54 Central Quartet Theorem
Theorem 7.20 — Exact content of the
functional symmetry
For every nontrivial zero \rho of \xi:

 \overline\rho,
\quad
1-\rho,
\quad
1-\overline\rho
are also zeros.
This symmetry implies the Riemann Hypothesis if and only
if every zero is fixed by the mirror map
\rho\mapsto1-\overline\rho.

Proof
The first statement follows from conjugation and the
functional equation.
The mirror fixed-point condition is
\rho=1-\overline\rho,
equivalent to
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12.
Thus the hypothesis is precisely the assertion that every zero
is a fixed point rather than a member of a distinct mirror pair.
∎
This isolates the unresolved step exactly.

 7.55 Conditional Positive-Energy
Theorem
Theorem 7.21 — What would be sufficient
Suppose one constructs a convergent functional
\mathcal E
=
\sum_\rho
w(\rho)
\left(
\operatorname{Re}\rho-\frac12
\right)^2,
with
w(\rho)>0,
and proves independently—without assuming the Riemann
Hypothesis—that
\mathcal E=0.
Then the Riemann Hypothesis follows.

Proof
Every term is nonnegative. A sum of nonnegative terms
equals zero only if every term vanishes. Therefore
\operatorname{Re}\rho=\frac12

 for every zero. ∎
The difficulty is the independent proof that \mathcal E=0, not
the final implication.

7.56 Proof Boundaries
This chapter establishes:
• the completed zeta functional equation and conjugation
symmetry;
• the critical line as the fixed set of mirror reflection;
• exact vanishing of the proposed symmetry-defect
operator;
• the impossibility of using that defect to localize zeros;
• quartet symmetry of off-line zeros;
• the logical distinction between symmetry and fixedpoint confinement;
• logarithmic-potential and Hadamard-product
interpretations;
• local behavior of |\xi|^2 near simple zeros;
• why every simple zero is locally a minimum of |\xi|^2;
• how off-line symmetric pairs affect transverse curvature;
• why zeros cannot cancel one another in an entire
product;
• how signed statistics may cancel while positive squared
displacement cannot;
• the limitations of finite numerical verification;

 • the correct burden for spectral, positivity, or
contradiction proofs;
• a precise non-circularity checklist;
• sufficient—but not yet established—positive-energy
criteria equivalent to the hypothesis.
It does not prove the Riemann Hypothesis. It proves which
symmetry-based approaches are valid, which are identically
empty, and what additional theorem would actually be
required.

8.3 Eigenvalues of the Fibonacci
Matrix
The characteristic polynomial of A is
\det(A-\lambda I)
=
\lambda^2-\lambda-1.
Its roots are
\lambda_\pm
=
\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}.

 Define
\varphi
=
\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
and
\psi
=
\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}
=
-\varphi^{-1}.

Theorem 8.2 — Golden-ratio spectrum
The Fibonacci companion matrix has eigenvalues
\varphi
and
-\varphi^{-1}.

Proof
Direct solution of the quadratic equation. ∎

8.4 Eigenvectors
For eigenvalue \lambda, solve

 A
\begin{bmatrix}
x\\y
\end{bmatrix}
=
\lambda
\begin{bmatrix}
x\\y
\end{bmatrix}.
The second row gives
x=\lambda y.
Choose
y=1,
so an eigenvector is
q_\lambda
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\lambda\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
Therefore
q_\varphi
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\varphi\\

 1
\end{bmatrix},
and
q_\psi
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\psi\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.

8.5 Diagonalization
Let
P
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\varphi&\psi\\
1&1
\end{bmatrix}.
Then
A
=
P
\begin{bmatrix}
\varphi&0\\
0&\psi

 \end{bmatrix}
P^{-1}.
Hence
A^n
=
P
\begin{bmatrix}
\varphi^n&0\\
0&\psi^n
\end{bmatrix}
P^{-1}.
This gives a closed form for the Fibonacci sequence.

8.6 Binet’s Formula
Theorem 8.3 — Exact closed form
F_n
=
\frac{
\varphi^n-\psi^n
}{
\sqrt5
}.

Proof

 Because the recurrence has characteristic roots \varphi and
\psi, every solution has the form
F_n=c_1\varphi^n+c_2\psi^n.
The initial conditions give
0=c_1+c_2,
and
1=c_1\varphi+c_2\psi.
Thus
c_2=-c_1,
and
1=c_1(\varphi-\psi).
Since
\varphi-\psi=\sqrt5,
c_1=\frac1{\sqrt5},
\qquad
c_2=-\frac1{\sqrt5}.
∎

8.7 Asymptotic Ratio
Theorem 8.4 — Fibonacci ratio convergence

 \lim_{n\to\infty}
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
=
\varphi.

Proof
Using Binet’s formula,
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
=
\frac{
\varphi^{n+1}-\psi^{n+1}
}{
\varphi^n-\psi^n
}.
Divide numerator and denominator by \varphi^n:
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
=
\frac{
\varphi-\psi(\psi/\varphi)^n
}{
1-(\psi/\varphi)^n
}.
Since
\left|\frac\psi\varphi\right|
=
\varphi^{-2}<1,

 the correction tends to zero. ∎

8.8 Exact Error Bound
From Binet’s formula,
F_n
=
\frac{\varphi^n}{\sqrt5}
\frac{\psi^n}{\sqrt5}.
Since
|\psi|<1,
\left|
F_n-\frac{\varphi^n}{\sqrt5}
\right|
=
\frac{|\psi|^n}{\sqrt5}
<
\frac12
for all n\ge1.

Corollary 8.5 — Nearest-integer formula
F_n
=
\left\lfloor

 \frac{\varphi^n}{\sqrt5}
+
\frac12
\right\rfloor.

8.9 Fibonacci Addition Formula
Theorem 8.6
For integers m\ge1 and n\ge0,
F_{m+n}
=
F_{m-1}F_n
+
F_mF_{n+1}.

Proof by induction on n
For n=0,
F_m
=
F_{m-1}F_0+F_mF_1
=
F_m.
Assume the identity holds for n and n-1. Then
\begin{aligned}
F_{m+n+1}

 &=
F_{m+n}+F_{m+n-1}\\
&=
F_{m-1}(F_n+F_{n-1})
+
F_m(F_{n+1}+F_n)\\
&=
F_{m-1}F_{n+1}
+
F_mF_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
∎

8.10 Doubling Identities
Set m=n in the addition formula:
F_{2n}
=
F_n(F_{n-1}+F_{n+1}).
Because
F_{n-1}+F_{n+1}
=
2F_{n+1}-F_n,
F_{2n}
=
F_n(2F_{n+1}-F_n).

 Also,
F_{2n+1}
=
F_n^2+F_{n+1}^2.
These formulas support fast doubling algorithms.

8.11 Cassini’s Identity
Theorem 8.7 — Cassini
F_{n+1}F_{n-1}-F_n^2
=
(-1)^n.

Proof using determinants
Since
\det A=-1,
\det A^n=(-1)^n.
A standard power formula is
A^n
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+1}&F_n\\
F_n&F_{n-1}
\end{bmatrix}.

 Therefore
\det A^n
=
F_{n+1}F_{n-1}-F_n^2
=
(-1)^n.
∎
Cassini’s identity expresses an alternating residual of exact
magnitude one.

8.12 Matrix-Power Formula
Theorem 8.8
For n\ge1,
A^n
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+1}&F_n\\
F_n&F_{n-1}
\end{bmatrix}.

Proof by induction
For n=1,
A
=

 \begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_2&F_1\\
F_1&F_0
\end{bmatrix}.
Assume true for n. Then
A^{n+1}
=
A^nA
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+1}+F_n&F_{n+1}\\
F_n+F_{n-1}&F_n
\end{bmatrix},
which equals
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+2}&F_{n+1}\\
F_{n+1}&F_n
\end{bmatrix}.
∎

 8.13 General Second-Order
Recurrence
Consider
x_{n+1}
=
ax_n+bx_{n-1}.
The companion matrix is
A_{a,b}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
a&b\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}.
Its characteristic equation is
\lambda^2-a\lambda-b=0.
The qualitative behavior depends on:
• the spectral radius;
• whether the roots are real or complex;
• multiplicity;
• initial conditions.
Fibonacci recursion is the special case
a=b=1.

 8.14 Stability Classification
For
v_{n+1}=Av_n,
the origin is asymptotically stable if
\rho(A)<1.
The Fibonacci matrix has
\rho(A)=\varphi>1,
so unnormalized Fibonacci recursion grows exponentially.
A normalized recurrence may be defined by
\widehat v_n
=
\varphi^{-n}v_n.
Then the dominant mode becomes stationary and the
conjugate mode decays as
\left(
-\varphi^{-2}
\right)^n.

8.15 Projective Convergence
Let

 r_n
=
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}.
Then
r_{n+1}
=
1+\frac1{r_n}.
Define
T(r)
=
1+\frac1r.
Its fixed points satisfy
r=1+\frac1r,
so
r^2-r-1=0.
The positive fixed point is \varphi.

Proposition 8.9 — Local contraction at
\varphi
T'(r)
=
-\frac1{r^2}.

 Therefore
|T'(\varphi)|
=
\varphi^{-2}<1.
Hence \varphi is locally attracting on the positive real line.

8.16 Möbius-Map Interpretation
The ratio update
T(r)
=
\frac{r+1}{r}
is a Möbius transformation represented projectively by the
Fibonacci matrix
A
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}.
Thus the golden-ratio fixed point is the projective
eigenvector direction of the recurrence matrix.

8.17 Modular Fibonacci Sequences

 Fix an integer modulus
m\ge2.
Consider the Fibonacci sequence modulo m:
F_n\bmod m.
The recurrence state is the ordered pair
(F_{n+1},F_n)\bmod m.
There are only
m^2
possible ordered pairs.

Theorem 8.10 — Eventual periodicity
The Fibonacci sequence modulo m is eventually periodic.

Proof
The pair-state evolves deterministically in a finite state space
of size m^2. Therefore some pair must repeat. From that
repetition onward, deterministic evolution repeats cyclically.
∎

8.18 Pure Periodicity
Because

 A
is invertible modulo m whenever
\gcd(\det A,m)=1,
and
\det A=-1,
the map is invertible modulo every m.

Theorem 8.11 — No transient
The Fibonacci sequence modulo m is purely periodic from
the initial pair
(1,0).

Proof
The state transition is bijective on the finite pair space
because -1 is invertible modulo m.
A repeated state therefore lies on a cycle with no non-cyclic
transient. Since the initial state itself has a predecessor, it
belongs to the cycle. ∎
The period is called the Pisano period.

8.19 Period Bound

 Because the nonzero reachable pair states lie inside a set of at
most
m^2
elements,
\pi(m)\le m^2
is an immediate crude bound.
Sharper bounds depend on number-theoretic structure.

8.20 Closure as State Return
For a deterministic recurrence
z_{n+1}=T(z_n),
define closure after N steps by
z_N=z_0.

Definition 8.1 — Exact discrete closure
The orbit closes with period N if
T^N(z_0)=z_0
and N is the least positive integer with this property.
For Fibonacci recursion over the integers, the unnormalized
orbit does not close except at the zero state.

 Modulo m, closure occurs because the state space is finite.

8.21 Residual Closure
In continuous or floating-point settings, exact return may be
replaced by a residual
\varepsilon_N
=
\|T^N(z_0)-z_0\|.
Define normalized closure error
\eta_N
=
\frac{
\|T^N(z_0)-z_0\|
}{
1+\|z_0\|
}.
A small residual indicates approximate return under the
chosen norm and representation.
It does not imply exact periodicity unless a theorem converts
the numerical bound into an exact statement.

8.22 Spectral Condition for Linear
Closure

 For
z_{n+1}=Az_n,
exact closure after N steps requires
A^Nz_0=z_0.
If closure is required for every initial state, then
A^N=I.

Theorem 8.12 — Eigenvalue condition
If A is diagonalizable and
A^N=I,
then every eigenvalue of A is an N-th root of unity.

Proof
For an eigenvector v,
Av=\lambda v.
Then
A^Nv=\lambda^Nv.
Because A^N=I,
\lambda^Nv=v,
so
\lambda^N=1.

 ∎
The Fibonacci eigenvalue \varphi is not a root of unity, so the
real Fibonacci transfer matrix cannot generate exact finite
closure.

8.23 Normalized Fibonacci Closure
Define
B
=
\varphi^{-1}A.
Its eigenvalues are
1
and
-\varphi^{-2}.
Repeated application converges toward the dominant
eigenline rather than cycling.

Theorem 8.13 — Rank-one asymptotic
closure
B^n
\rightarrow
P_\varphi

 as n\to\infty, where P_\varphi is the spectral projector onto
the golden-ratio eigenvector.

Proof
Diagonalization gives
B^n
=
P
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0\\
0&(-\varphi^{-2})^n
\end{bmatrix}
P^{-1}.
The second eigenvalue tends to zero. ∎
This is asymptotic directional stabilization, not periodic
closure.

8.24 Fibonacci Words
Define words over an alphabet \{A,B\} by
W_0=B,
\qquad
W_1=A,
and
W_{n+1}=W_nW_{n-1}.

 Then the word length satisfies
|W_{n+1}|
=
|W_n|+|W_{n-1}|.
With the chosen initial conditions,
|W_n|=F_{n+1}.

Theorem 8.14 — Fibonacci word length
|W_n|=F_{n+1}.

Proof
The lengths satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence with
|W_0|=1=F_1,
and
|W_1|=1=F_2.
Uniqueness of recurrence solutions gives the result. ∎

8.25 Symbol Counts
Let
a_n
be the number of A symbols in W_n, and

 b_n
the number of B symbols.
Then
a_{n+1}=a_n+a_{n-1},
and
b_{n+1}=b_n+b_{n-1}.
From the initial words,
a_n=F_n,
\qquad
b_n=F_{n-1}
for appropriate indexing.
Hence the frequency ratio approaches \varphi.

8.26 Substitution Rule
The infinite Fibonacci word can be generated by the
substitution
A\mapsto AB,
B\mapsto A.
The substitution matrix is

 S
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix},
the same Fibonacci matrix.
The Perron–Frobenius eigenvector determines the
asymptotic symbol frequencies.

8.27 Symbol Frequencies
The positive eigenvector is
\begin{bmatrix}
\varphi\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
Normalize by the sum
\varphi+1=\varphi^2.
Therefore the asymptotic frequencies are
f_A
=
\frac{\varphi}{\varphi^2}
=
\frac1{\varphi},

 and
f_B
=
\frac1{\varphi^2}.
They sum to one because
\varphi^{-1}+\varphi^{-2}=1.

8.28 Fibonacci Braid Recursion
Let B_N be a braid group.
Choose two braid elements
X,Y\in B_N.
Define recursively
\beta_0=Y,
\qquad
\beta_1=X,
and
\beta_{n+1}
=
\beta_n\beta_{n-1}.
This is a group-valued Fibonacci recursion.

 Because braid multiplication is generally noncommutative,
order matters.

8.29 Exponent Sum Recurrence
Apply the braid-group abelianization
e:B_N\rightarrow\mathbb Z.
Then
e(\beta_{n+1})
=
e(\beta_n)+e(\beta_{n-1}).

Theorem 8.15 — Fibonacci exponent sum
If
e(\beta_0)=p,
\qquad
e(\beta_1)=q,
then
e(\beta_n)
=
F_nq+F_{n-1}p
for n\ge1.

Proof

 The exponent sum converts braid multiplication into integer
addition, so the sequence satisfies the ordinary Fibonacci
recurrence with the stated initial values. ∎
The full braid element contains more information than its
exponent sum.

8.30 Noncommutative Word Growth
Let \ell(\beta) denote unreduced word length in a fixed
generating representation.
Before simplification,
\ell(\beta_{n+1})
=
\ell(\beta_n)+\ell(\beta_{n-1}).
After applying braid relations and cancellation,
\ell_{\min}(\beta_{n+1})
\le
\ell_{\min}(\beta_n)
+
\ell_{\min}(\beta_{n-1}).
Equality need not hold.

8.31 Matrix Representation of
Braids

 Let
\rho:B_N\rightarrow GL(k,\mathbb C)
be a representation.
Then
M_n
=
\rho(\beta_n)
satisfies
M_{n+1}
=
M_nM_{n-1}.
This is a nonlinear matrix recurrence because matrix

Its behavior depends on:
•

noncommutativity;
spectral radii;
common invariant subspaces;
representation parameters.

8.32 Commuting Case
If
M_0M_1=M_1M_0,

 then all matrices generated by the recursion commute.
In a simultaneous eigenbasis, each scalar eigenvalue
sequence satisfies
\mu_{n+1}
=
\mu_n\mu_{n-1}.
Taking logarithms where defined,
y_n=\log\mu_n
gives
y_{n+1}=y_n+y_{n-1}.
Thus
y_n
=
F_ny_1+F_{n-1}y_0.
Therefore
\mu_n
=
\mu_1^{F_n}
\mu_0^{F_{n-1}}.

8.33 The Multiplicative Fibonacci
Recurrence

 Consider positive scalars satisfying
x_{n+1}=x_nx_{n-1}.

Theorem 8.16
x_n
=
x_1^{F_n}
x_0^{F_{n-1}}
for n\ge1.

Proof
Take logarithms and apply the additive Fibonacci solution, or
prove directly by induction. ∎
This recurrence typically grows far faster than ordinary
Fibonacci numbers when x_0,x_1>1.

8.34 Braid Closure
A braid \beta\in B_N can be closed by connecting
corresponding top and bottom strand endpoints.
Denote the closure by
\widehat\beta.
Different braid words may have isotopic closures.

 Markov’s theorem characterizes when two braids have
equivalent closures through:
• conjugation;
• stabilization and destabilization.
Thus equality of braid-group elements is stronger than
equality of closed links.

8.35 Recursive Braid Closure
For recursively generated braids \beta_n, one may ask
whether
\widehat{\beta_n}
eventually repeats up to isotopy.
This is not implied by Fibonacci recurrence.
A proof would require:
• a finite quotient representation;
• periodicity in an invariant;
• or a direct Markov-equivalence argument.

8.36 Finite Quotient Periodicity
Suppose a group homomorphism maps
\rho:B_N\rightarrow G
into a finite group G.

 Then the pair state
(\rho(\beta_n),\rho(\beta_{n-1}))
lies in the finite set
G\times G.

Theorem 8.17 — Eventual periodicity in a
finite quotient
The recursive braid sequence is eventually periodic after
projection into any finite group representation.

Proof
The pair update is deterministic on a finite state space. ∎
This establishes periodicity of the quotient image, not of the
full braid sequence.

8.37 Transfer Matrices
A local strand rule may be encoded by transfer matrices
T_A,
\qquad
T_B.
For a word
W=s_1s_2\cdots s_n,

 define
T(W)
=
T_{s_n}\cdots T_{s_1},
with order chosen according to propagation convention.
For Fibonacci words,
W_{n+1}=W_nW_{n-1},
so
T_{n+1}
=
T_{n-1}T_n
or the reversed product, depending on convention.
Order must be fixed explicitly.

8.38 Trace Map
For certain unimodular 2\times2 transfer matrices, define
x_n
=
\frac12\operatorname{tr}T_n.
Under Fibonacci multiplication, traces may satisfy a
nonlinear recurrence of the form

 x_{n+1}
=
2x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-2}.
This is the Fibonacci trace map.
Its precise derivation requires:
• determinant-one matrices;
• the specific multiplication convention;
• the Cayley–Hamilton identity.

8.39 Cayley–Hamilton Identity for
SL(2)
Let
M\in SL(2,\mathbb C).
Then
M^2-(\operatorname{tr}M)M+I=0.
Therefore
M^{-1}
=
(\operatorname{tr}M)I-M.
This identity is central to deriving trace recurrences.

8.40 Fricke Identity

 For
A,B\in SL(2,\mathbb C),
define
x=\frac12\operatorname{tr}A,
y=\frac12\operatorname{tr}B,
z=\frac12\operatorname{tr}(AB).
The commutator trace is related to
x^2+y^2+z^2-2xyz.
Depending on normalization,
\operatorname{tr}
(ABA^{-1}B^{-1})
determines an invariant surface for the trace map.
This structure appears in quasiperiodic transfer problems.

8.41 Fibonacci Trace-Map Invariant
For the recurrence
x_{n+1}
=
2x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-2},
define

 I_n
=
x_{n+1}^2+x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2
2x_{n+1}x_nx_{n-1}
1.

Theorem 8.18 — Trace-map invariant
I_n=I_{n-1}.

Proof
Substitute
x_{n+1}=2x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-2}
into I_n, expand, and collect terms. The expression reduces
exactly to
x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2+x_{n-2}^2
2x_nx_{n-1}x_{n-2}
1
