I_{n-1}.
∎
This is a genuine conserved residual for the trace recurrence.

 8.42 Residual Closure Functional
for Recurrences
Given a recurrence state
z_n,
define an invariant candidate
I(z_n).
The residual is
r_n
=
I(z_{n+1})-I(z_n).
Exact closure of the invariant means
r_n=0
for all n.
Numerically, report
|r_n|
and compare it with precision and conditioning.
A small invariant residual does not imply the full state has
closed.

 8.43 State Closure Versus Invariant
Closure
Proposition 8.19
It is possible that
I(z_{n+1})=I(z_n)
for every n, while
z_{n+1}\neq z_n.

Proof by example
A rotation on the unit circle preserves
I(x,y)=x^2+y^2,
but changes the state at every nontrivial angle. ∎
An invariant constrains motion to a level set; it does not
imply stationarity or periodicity.

8.44 Fibonacci Residues and Strand
Labels
Suppose strand labels are assigned by

 \ell_n
=
F_n\bmod m.
Then the label sequence is periodic with Pisano period
\pi(m).
This can produce repeating strand classes or colors.
However, periodic labels do not imply the geometric strands
close in space.
A spatial embedding map must also return to its initial
position and orientation.

8.45 Discrete Geometric Strand
Model
Let a strand position satisfy
x_{n+1}
=
x_n
+
R(\theta_n)\,d_n,
where:
• R(\theta_n) is a rotation;
• d_n is a step vector;
• \theta_n may be determined by Fibonacci residues.

 Exact closure after N steps requires
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
R(\theta_n)d_n
=
0,
and orientation closure requires
\theta_N-\theta_0
\in2\pi\mathbb Z.
Both conditions are necessary.

8.46 Polygonal Closure Theorem
Theorem 8.20
A discrete strand with increments
\Delta x_n
closes after N steps if and only if
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta x_n=0.

Proof
By telescoping,
x_N-x_0
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}

 (x_{n+1}-x_n)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta x_n.
Thus x_N=x_0 exactly when the sum vanishes. ∎
This is the exact vector closure condition.

8.47 Root-of-Unity Closure
Suppose planar increments are
\Delta z_n
=
a_n e^{i\theta_n}.
If all lengths are equal,
a_n=a,
and angles run through all N-th roots of unity,
\theta_n
=
\theta_0+\frac{2\pi n}{N},
then
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Delta z_n
=
ae^{i\theta_0}
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
e^{2\pi in/N}

 =
0.
Thus a regular polygon closes.
A Fibonacci angular sequence generally does not produce
uniform roots of unity unless reduced modulo a suitable
period and balanced.

8.48 Weighted Root-of-Unity Sum
For arbitrary weights a_n, closure requires
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
a_n\omega^n
=
0,
\qquad
\omega=e^{2\pi i/N}.
This is a discrete Fourier coefficient condition.
Fibonacci weights do not generally satisfy it automatically.

8.49 Generating Function
The Fibonacci generating function is
G(x)
=

 \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
F_nx^n.

Theorem 8.21
For |x|<\varphi^{-1},
G(x)
=
\frac{x}{1-x-x^2}.

Proof
Using the recurrence,
\begin{aligned}
G(x)-x
&=
\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}F_nx^n\\
&=
\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(F_{n-1}+F_{n-2})x^n\\
&=
x\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}F_nx^n
+
x^2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}F_nx^n\\
&=
xG(x)+x^2G(x).
\end{aligned}
Therefore
G(x)(1-x-x^2)=x.

 ∎
The poles occur at
x=\varphi^{-1}
and
x=-\varphi.
The nearest pole to the origin determines the growth rate.

8.50 Zeckendorf Representation
Every positive integer can be represented uniquely as a sum
of nonconsecutive Fibonacci numbers.

Theorem 8.22 — Zeckendorf’s theorem
For every integer N\ge1, there exists a unique representation
N
=
F_{k_1}+F_{k_2}+\cdots+F_{k_r},
with
k_j-k_{j+1}\ge2
and Fibonacci indexing beginning with distinct positive
terms.

Proof outline

 Existence: Apply the greedy algorithm, repeatedly
subtracting the largest Fibonacci number not exceeding the
remainder. The recurrence guarantees that the next chosen
term is nonconsecutive.
Uniqueness: Assume two distinct nonconsecutive
representations. Compare their largest differing Fibonacci
term and use
F_k
>
F_{k-1}+F_{k-3}+F_{k-5}+\cdots
to show smaller nonconsecutive terms cannot compensate for
it. ∎
This theorem creates a unique Fibonacci coding of integers,
but does not automatically imply geometric or physical
encoding.

8.51 Fibonacci Convolution
Theorem 8.23
\sum_{k=0}^{n}
F_kF_{n-k}
=
\frac{
nL_n-F_n
}{5},

 where L_n is the Lucas sequence.
Such convolution identities arise when two Fibonaccirecursive channels interact linearly.
Their physical relevance depends on the coupling model.

8.52 Lucas Sequence
Define
L_0=2,
\qquad
L_1=1,
and
L_{n+1}=L_n+L_{n-1}.
Then
L_n=\varphi^n+\psi^n.
Also,
L_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n+1}.
The Lucas sequence supplies the trace of the Fibonacci
matrix:
\operatorname{tr}A^n=L_n.

8.53 Determinant and Trace

 From
A^n
=
\begin{bmatrix}
F_{n+1}&F_n\\
F_n&F_{n-1}
\end{bmatrix},
\operatorname{tr}A^n
=
F_{n+1}+F_{n-1}
=
L_n.
And
\det A^n=(-1)^n.
Therefore the powers alternate orientation in two dimensions
while growing along the dominant eigenvector.

8.54 Fibonacci Rotation Is Not
Automatic
The Fibonacci companion matrix is not orthogonal:
A^TA
\neq I.
Its eigenvalues are real, not unit modulus.

 Therefore it produces stretching and contraction, not pure
rotation.
Any claim that Fibonacci recursion generates geometric
rotation requires an additional mapping, normalization, or
phase embedding.

8.55 Phase Embedding
One possible phase embedding is
\theta_n
=
2\pi
\{n\varphi\},
where \{\cdot\} denotes fractional part.
Because \varphi is irrational, the sequence is equidistributed
modulo one.

Theorem 8.24 — Irrational rotation density
The sequence
n\varphi\bmod1
is dense in [0,1).

Proof

 This is a standard result for irrational rotations on the circle.
If the orbit were not dense, it would contradict the
minimality of irrational circle rotation. ∎
Density is not periodic closure.

8.56 Golden-Angle Sequence
The golden angle is commonly defined modulo 2\pi by
\alpha_g
=
2\pi
\left(
1-\frac1\varphi
\right)
=
\frac{2\pi}{\varphi^2}.
The sequence
\theta_n=n\alpha_g\bmod2\pi
is nonperiodic because
\frac{\alpha_g}{2\pi}
=
\varphi^{-2}
is irrational.

 It distributes points evenly in an asymptotic sense but never
returns exactly.

8.57 Exact Versus Quasiperiodic
Closure
Theorem 8.25
A circle rotation
\theta_{n+1}
=
\theta_n+\alpha
\pmod{2\pi}
has an exact finite period if and only if
\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\in\mathbb Q.

Proof
Exact period N requires
N\alpha=2\pi k
for some integer k, equivalent to rationality.
Conversely, if
\alpha/(2\pi)=p/q,
then period divides q. ∎

 Golden-angle dynamics are quasiperiodic, not exactly
periodic.

8.58 Approximate Return
For irrational rotations, Dirichlet approximation guarantees
integers p,q such that
\left|
q\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}-p
\right|
<
\frac1q.
Thus arbitrarily close returns exist, but exact return does not.
A numerical closure residual must therefore be interpreted
against Diophantine approximation.

8.59 Fibonacci Approximants to
\varphi
The convergents of the continued fraction
\varphi=[1;1,1,1,\ldots]
are
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}.

 Theorem 8.26 — Approximation error
\left|
\varphi-\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
\right|
=
\frac1{
F_n(\varphi F_n+F_{n-1})
}.
In particular,
\left|
\varphi-\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
\right|
<
\frac1{F_n^2}.

Proof
Use Cassini’s identity or Binet’s formula to evaluate the
difference exactly. ∎
This explains why Fibonacci numbers generate especially
close rational approximations to golden-ratio rotations.

8.60 Near-Closure from Fibonacci
Approximants
Let

 \alpha
=
\frac{2\pi}{\varphi}.
After F_n steps,
F_n\alpha
=
2\pi\frac{F_n}{\varphi}.
Because
\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}
\approx\varphi,
\frac{F_n}{\varphi}
\approx
F_{n-1}.
Thus the phase nearly returns modulo 2\pi.
The residual decreases exponentially with n, but never
becomes exactly zero.

8.61 Exact Near-Return Identity
Using
F_n\varphi
=
F_{n+1}

 (-\varphi)^{-n},
one obtains
\frac{F_n}{\varphi}
=
F_{n-1}
+
(-1)^{n-1}\varphi^{-n}.
Therefore
F_n\frac{2\pi}{\varphi}
=
2\pi F_{n-1}
+
2\pi(-1)^{n-1}\varphi^{-n}.
Modulo 2\pi, the residual phase is
\Delta\theta_n
=
2\pi(-1)^{n-1}\varphi^{-n}.

Theorem 8.27 — Exponentially small
Fibonacci near-closure
The F_n-step residual of rotation by 2\pi/\varphi has
magnitude

 |\Delta\theta_n|
=
2\pi\varphi^{-n}.

Proof
From the exact identity above. ∎
This is a mathematically precise form of residual closure
generated by Fibonacci approximants.

8.62 Alternating Mirror Residual
The sign
(-1)^{n-1}
in the near-return residual alternates.
Therefore successive Fibonacci approximants approach the
target angle from alternating sides.
This is an arithmetic mirror behavior, not a spatial parity
transformation unless a geometric embedding is specified.

8.63 Fibonacci Spiral Geometry
A common geometric construction places points at radius
r_n=c\sqrt n
and angle

 \theta_n=n\alpha_g.
This produces phyllotactic patterns with approximate
uniform density.
The square-root radial law is not derived from the Fibonacci
recurrence itself. It is an additional geometric design choice.

8.64 Logarithmic Golden Spiral
A logarithmic spiral satisfies
r(\theta)=r_0e^{k\theta}.
If the radius scales by \varphi after a quarter turn,
r\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
=
\varphi r(\theta),
then
e^{k\pi/2}=\varphi,
so
k=\frac{2\log\varphi}{\pi}.
This is one precise definition of a golden spiral.
It is not the same object as the Fibonacci sequence, though
finite square constructions approximate it visually.

 8.65 Fibonacci Tiling Recursion
Suppose a geometric assembly contains counts
N_A(n),
\qquad
N_B(n)
of two tile types, updated by
\begin{bmatrix}
N_A(n+1)\\
N_B(n+1)
\end{bmatrix}
=
A
\begin{bmatrix}
N_A(n)\\
N_B(n)
\end{bmatrix}.
Then tile-count ratios approach \varphi.
This proves asymptotic composition, not geometric selfsimilarity unless the substitution also specifies tile shapes
and matching rules.

8.66 Recursive Strand-Length
Model

 Suppose strand lengths satisfy
L_{n+1}=L_n+L_{n-1}.
Then
L_n
=
F_nL_1+F_{n-1}L_0.
If L_0,L_1>0,
\frac{L_{n+1}}{L_n}\rightarrow\varphi.
The recurrence predicts length ratios only. Curvature,
embedding, contact, and topology require separate equations.

8.67 Energy Recurrence
If energy contributions obey
E_{n+1}=E_n+E_{n-1},
then
E_n
=
F_nE_1+F_{n-1}E_0.
This is mathematically exact given the recurrence.

 But a physical theory must derive why energies add in this
manner. Energies of interacting structures usually include
cross terms.

8.68 Coupled Recurrence with
Interaction
A more realistic model is
E_{n+1}
=
E_n+E_{n-1}
+
C(E_n,E_{n-1}),
where C is an interaction correction.
The ordinary Fibonacci law holds only if
C\equiv0.
Thus observed deviation from Fibonacci scaling may
quantify coupling rather than failure of recursion.

8.69 Residual from Fibonacci
Prediction
Define

 r_n
=
x_{n+1}-x_n-x_{n-1}.
Exact Fibonacci recursion means
r_n=0.
A normalized residual is
\widehat r_n
=
\frac{
x_{n+1}-x_n-x_{n-1}
}{
|x_{n+1}|+|x_n|+|x_{n-1}|+\epsilon
}.
This can be used as a model diagnostic.
A small residual shows approximate recurrence, not why the
recurrence occurs.

8.70 Least-Squares Recurrence Fit
Given data x_0,\ldots,x_N, fit
x_{n+1}=ax_n+bx_{n-1}
by minimizing
J(a,b)
=

 \sum_{n=1}^{N-1}
\left(
x_{n+1}-ax_n-bx_{n-1}
\right)^2.
The normal equations are
\begin{bmatrix}
\sum x_n^2&
\sum x_nx_{n-1}\\
\sum x_nx_{n-1}&
\sum x_{n-1}^2
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
a\\b
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sum x_nx_{n+1}\\
\sum x_{n-1}x_{n+1}
\end{bmatrix}.
A fitted result near
a=b=1
supports a Fibonacci-like model within the dataset, subject to
uncertainty and model comparison.

8.71 Statistical Test Boundary

 A visual pattern resembling Fibonacci growth is insufficient.
A defensible test should compare:
• Fibonacci recurrence;
• alternative linear recurrences;
• exponential growth;
• polynomial growth;
• stochastic models.
Model selection should report uncertainty, residuals, out-ofsample prediction, and sensitivity.

8.72 Recursive Closure on a Graph
Let graph states satisfy
x_{n+1}=A_Gx_n+A_Gx_{n-1},
where A_G is a graph operator.
Lift to first order:
\begin{bmatrix}
x_{n+1}\\
x_n
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
A_G&A_G\\
I&0
\end{bmatrix}

 \begin{bmatrix}
x_n\\
x_{n-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
The spectrum of the lifted operator determines growth and
closure.
If \mu is an eigenvalue of A_G, the corresponding lifted
eigenvalues satisfy
\lambda^2-\mu\lambda-\mu=0.
Exact periodic closure requires these \lambda values to be
roots of unity on the excited modes.

8.73 No-Go for Positive Graph
Eigenvalues
If \mu>0, one lifted root is
\lambda_+
=
\frac{
\mu+\sqrt{\mu^2+4\mu}
}{2}
>1.
Therefore the corresponding mode grows and cannot be
periodic without normalization or nonlinear saturation.

 8.74 Nonlinear Saturated Fibonacci
Map
One may define
x_{n+1}
=
\tanh
\left(
ax_n+bx_{n-1}
\right).
This remains bounded.
Fixed points satisfy
x=\tanh((a+b)x).
Stability depends on the Jacobian
J
=
\begin{bmatrix}
a\,\operatorname{sech}^2(\cdot)&
b\,\operatorname{sech}^2(\cdot)\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}.
The presence of Fibonacci-like coupling coefficients does
not determine the nonlinear dynamics by itself.

 8.75 Recursive Braid Energy
Let a braid recursion be
\beta_{n+1}
=
\beta_n\beta_{n-1}.
Suppose an energy-like functional E is subadditive under
composition:
E(\alpha\beta)
\le
E(\alpha)+E(\beta).
Then
E(\beta_{n+1})
\le
E(\beta_n)+E(\beta_{n-1}).

Proposition 8.28 — Fibonacci upper bound
If
E_n=E(\beta_n),
then
E_n
\le
F_nE_1+F_{n-1}E_0.

 Proof
Induct using the subadditive recurrence inequality. ∎
Equality requires exact additivity and no cancellation or
relaxation.

8.76 Submultiplicative Matrix Norm
Bound
For a matrix representation,
M_{n+1}
=
M_nM_{n-1}.
Using a submultiplicative norm,
\|M_{n+1}\|
\le
\|M_n\|
\|M_{n-1}\|.
Taking logarithms,
y_n=\log\|M_n\|
gives
y_{n+1}
\le
y_n+y_{n-1}.

 Therefore
y_n
\le
F_ny_1+F_{n-1}y_0
when the logarithms are nonnegative or interpreted carefully.
Thus matrix norm growth can be bounded by multiplicative
Fibonacci scaling.

8.77 Recursive Commutator
Residual
For noncommuting matrices, define
C_n
=
[M_n,M_{n-1}]
=
M_nM_{n-1}-M_{n-1}M_n.
If
C_n=0,
the adjacent recursion factors commute.
A small normalized commutator,
\chi_n
=

 \frac{
\|C_n\|
}{
\|M_n\|\|M_{n-1}\|+\epsilon
},
measures approximate commutativity.
Approximate commutativity may justify scalar spectral
approximations locally, but not exact diagonalization.

8.78 Recursive Orientation
If braid exponent sums satisfy
e_{n+1}=e_n+e_{n-1},
then sign may eventually become fixed if the dominant
golden-ratio mode has nonzero coefficient.
However, sign of exponent sum is not complete chirality.
Two braids with positive exponent sum may have different
mirror properties.

8.79 Closure in a Finite
Representation
Suppose
\rho(\beta_n)

 lies in a finite unitary group.
Then the pair-state recursion is periodic.
The resulting matrix closure period is at most
|G|^2.
This may be used to construct exact digital braid cycles.
It does not prove the underlying continuous braid geometry
is periodic.

8.80 Central Fibonacci Closure
Theorem
Theorem 8.29 — Exact arithmetic nearclosure under golden rotation
Let
\theta_n
=
n\frac{2\pi}{\varphi}
\pmod{2\pi}.
At Fibonacci times n=F_k,
\theta_{F_k}
=
2\pi

 (-1)^{k-1}
\varphi^{-k}
\pmod{2\pi}.
Therefore the closure residual decays exponentially:
|\theta_{F_k}|
=
2\pi\varphi^{-k}.

Proof
Use the exact identity
\frac{F_k}{\varphi}
=
F_{k-1}
+
(-1)^{k-1}\varphi^{-k}.
Multiply by 2\pi and reduce modulo 2\pi. ∎
This proves a precise residual-closure phenomenon
connecting Fibonacci numbers and golden-ratio rotation.
It is approximate closure, not exact periodicity.

8.81 Central Recurrence–Braid
Boundary Theorem
Theorem 8.30

 A Fibonacci recursion assigned to braid words determines:
1. a recursive algebraic sequence in the braid group;
2. Fibonacci growth of any additive homomorphic
invariant;
3. eventual periodicity in every finite quotient.
It does not, without further assumptions, determine:
1. geometric strand lengths;
2. spatial closure;
3. knot type of the closures;
4. physical energy;
5. stability;
6. material realization.

Proof
The first three properties follow from the group recursion
and homomorphism or finiteness arguments.
The remaining quantities depend on geometric embeddings,
closure operations, energy functionals, and physical
constitutive laws absent from the abstract recursion. ∎

where:

structure.

o_n

The agent produces:

a_n

This separates prediction, action, environment transition, and

 9.2 Prediction Residual
Define the prediction residual
r_n
=
o_{n+1}
\widehat o_{n+1}.
For vector observations, define residual energy
E_n
=
\frac12
r_n^TWr_n,
where
W=W^T\succ0.
The Euclidean case is recovered with
W=I.

Lemma 9.1 — Residual energy is nonnegative
E_n\ge0,
with equality if and only if
r_n=0.

 Proof
Since W\succ0,
r_n^TWr_n>0
for every nonzero r_n, while it is zero for r_n=0. ∎
The residual energy measures error under the chosen metric.
It does not by itself determine whether the prediction model
is scientifically correct outside the observed domain.

9.3 Residual Contraction
Suppose a candidate correction transforms the residual from
r_n to r_n^+.

Definition 9.1 — Contraction ratio
For E_n>0, define
\gamma_n
=
\frac{E_n^+}{E_n}.
The candidate is:
• strictly contracting if
0\le\gamma_n<1;
• neutral if
\gamma_n=1;

 • expanding if
\gamma_n>1.
Define verified improvement
\Delta E_n
=
E_n-E_n^+.
Then contraction is equivalent to
\Delta E_n>0.

Proposition 9.2 — Repeated uniform
contraction
Suppose
E_{n+1}\le\gamma E_n
for every n, where
0\le\gamma<1.
Then
E_n
\le
\gamma^nE_0,
and therefore
E_n\rightarrow0.

 Proof
Repeated substitution gives
E_n
\le
\gamma E_{n-1}
\le
\gamma^2E_{n-2}
\le
\cdots
\le
\gamma^nE_0.
Since \gamma^n\to0, the residual energy converges to zero. ∎

9.4 Nonuniform Contraction
Suppose
E_{n+1}
\le
\gamma_nE_n,
\qquad
0\le\gamma_n\le1.
Then
E_n
\le

 E_0
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma_k.

Theorem 9.3 — Product criterion
If
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
(1-\gamma_k)
=
\infty,
then
E_n\rightarrow0.

Proof
For 0<\gamma\le1,
\log\gamma
\le
-(1-\gamma).
Therefore
\log
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma_k
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\log\gamma_k
\le
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-\gamma_k).

 The right side tends to -\infty, so the product tends to zero. ∎
Strict improvement at every step is not enough by itself; the
total contraction must not become summably weak.

9.5 Residual Contraction Under
Disturbance
Suppose
E_{n+1}
\le
\gamma E_n+\varepsilon,
where
0\le\gamma<1,
\qquad
\varepsilon\ge0.

Theorem 9.4 — Error-floor bound
E_n
\le
\gamma^nE_0
+
\varepsilon
\frac{1-\gamma^n}{1-\gamma}.
Hence

 \limsup_{n\to\infty}E_n
\le
\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}.

Proof
Iterate the inequality:
E_n
\le
\gamma^nE_0
+
\varepsilon
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\gamma^j.
Evaluate the geometric sum. ∎
Persistent noise or model mismatch creates a residual floor

9.6 Candidate Scoring
Let c\in\mathcal C_n be a candidate correction.
Define its score
S_n(c)
=
w_E\Delta E_n(c)
+
w_G\Delta G_n(c)

 +
w_I I_n(c)
w_RR_n(c)
w_CC_n(c),
where:
• \Delta E_n(c) is residual reduction;
• \Delta G_n(c) is goal progress;
• I_n(c) is information gain;
• R_n(c) is estimated risk;
• C_n(c) is implementation cost;
• all weights are nonnegative.
A candidate is admissible only if it satisfies safety and
boundedness constraints.

Definition 9.2 — Pure candidate evaluation
Candidate scoring is pure if evaluating S_n(c) does not
modify:
• the live state;
• retained memory;
• adaptive parameters;
• the graph;
• the random-number state used for actual execution.
Purity prevents scoring order from changing the decision.

 Proposition 9.5 — Order independence under
pure scoring
If candidate evaluation is pure and deterministic, then the
selected maximizer
c_n^*
=
\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal C_n}S_n(c)
is independent of the order in which candidates are
evaluated, except for explicitly specified tie-breaking.

Proof
Pure evaluation assigns each candidate a fixed score
independent of prior evaluations. Therefore the set of scores
is invariant under enumeration order. ∎
Without pure scoring, candidate assessment can contaminate
the state and make the decision path dependent.

9.7 Promotion Gates
A candidate should not be promoted solely because it
improved one sample.
Define a promotion gate with conditions:
\mathsf G(c)=1
if and only if all of the following hold:

 \Delta E_n(c)\ge\delta_E,
R_n(c)\le R_{\max},
\|\Delta\theta(c)\|\le B_\theta,
\Delta G_n(c)\ge-\delta_G,
and
N_{\mathrm{success}}(c)\ge q
within a validation window of length w.
Otherwise,
\mathsf G(c)=0.
The thresholds must be defined before testing.

9.8 False Promotion Bound
Suppose a non-improving candidate passes an individual trial
by chance with probability at most p.
Assume independent validation trials.
If promotion requires q successes in q trials, then the falsepromotion probability is at most
p^q.

Theorem 9.6 — Repetition suppresses
accidental promotion

 Under the independence assumption,
P(\text{false promotion})
\le
p^q.

Proof
The probability that all q independent trials pass is the
product
p^q.
∎
The independence assumption is strong. Correlated
validation samples reduce the effective strength of repeated
testing.

9.9 Majority Promotion Gate
Suppose promotion requires at least q successes among w
independent trials.
If the false-success probability is p, then
P_{\mathrm{false}}
=
\sum_{k=q}^{w}
\binom wk
p^k(1-p)^{w-k}.

 This is the binomial tail.
For q>wp, concentration inequalities provide exponential
bounds.

Theorem 9.7 — Hoeffding false-promotion
bound
Let X_1,\ldots,X_w be independent Bernoulli variables with
mean at most p.
If promotion requires an empirical success rate at least
\tau>p, then
P
\left(
\frac1w\sum_{i=1}^{w}X_i
\ge\tau
\right)
\le
\exp
\left[
-2w(\tau-p)^2
\right].

Proof
Apply Hoeffding’s inequality to bounded independent
variables. ∎

 Repeated verified improvement provides statistical
protection only when the trial design is valid.

=

b_n.

This gives a formal contraction result for a specific class of

Nonconvex adaptive agents require weaker guarantees.

=
y_n+h k_1,
k_2
=

y_n
+
\frac h2
(k_1+k_2).

Heun’s Method
Assume f is sufficiently smooth.

Theorem 9.12 — Second-order accuracy
Heun’s method has local truncation error
O(h^3)
and global error
O(h^2)
over a fixed finite interval.

Proof sketch
Expand the exact solution:
y(t+h)
=
y

 +
hf
+
\frac{h^2}{2}
(f_t+f_yf)
+
O(h^3).
Expand
k_2
=
f(t+h,y+hf)
=
f
+
h(f_t+f_yf)
+
O(h^2).
Then
y_{n+1}
=
y
+
\frac h2
\left[
f+
f+h(f_t+f_yf)
\right]

 +
O(h^3),
which matches the exact Taylor expansion through h^2.

Apply Heun’s method to
\dot y=\lambda y.
Then
y_{n+1}
=
R(z)y_n,
\qquad
z=h\lambda,
where
R(z)
=
1+z+\frac{z^2}{2}.

Theorem 9.13 — Absolute stability criterion
The numerical solution contracts on the linear test equation
precisely when

 |R(z)|<1.

Proof
After n steps,
y_n=R(z)^ny_0.
This converges to zero exactly when the amplification
magnitude is less than one. ∎
A stable continuous system may be numerically destabilized
if the timestep places z outside the Heun stability region.

Let the internal state be
s=
\begin{bmatrix}
e\\x\\m
\end{bmatrix},
with dynamics

=

A representative leaky model is

=

=

=

1-h\lambda_j+\frac{h^2\lambda_j^2}{2}

\le
|a-b|.

Proof
Projection onto a closed interval is nonexpansive. ∎

9.19 Bounded Internal Blend
Suppose an internal scalar output is
b
=
w_e e+w_xx+w_mm,
where
|e|,|x|,|m|\le M.
Then
|b|
\le
M
\left(
|w_e|+|w_x|+|w_m|
\right).

|b|\le M.
Thus a convex blend preserves the component bound.

 9.20 Stable Graph Identity
Let a graph be
G=(V,E,\mu),
with node set V, edge multiset E, and metadata \mu.
A deterministic graph fingerprint should be invariant under
arbitrary storage order.
Define a canonical serialization:
1. convert every node and edge attribute to a deterministic
built-in representation;
2. sort nodes by canonical key;
3. normalize each undirected edge endpoint order;
4. sort edges lexicographically;
5. sort metadata keys;
6. serialize without nondeterministic whitespace;
7. hash the resulting byte string.

Theorem 9.15 — Order-invariant fingerprint
If two graph representations differ only by ordering of nodes,
edges, or metadata fields, their canonical fingerprints are
identical.

Proof

 Canonical sorting maps every equivalent ordering to the
same serialized sequence. Deterministic hashing then
produces the same digest. ∎

Proposition 9.16 — Fingerprint equality is
not graph-isomorphism proof
Two isomorphic graphs with different node labels can have
different canonical fingerprints unless the canonicalization
includes a label-independent graph-isomorphism procedure.

Proof
The serialization may preserve node labels. Relabeling
changes the serialized keys even though the abstract graphs
are isomorphic. ∎
A stable identity hash and a graph-isomorphism certificate
are different tools.

=

+

where

=
\sum_{k=0}^{n}
(\gamma\lambda)^{n-k}\phi_k
assuming e_{-1}=0.

Proof
Expand the recursion repeatedly or prove by induction. ∎
Recent features receive greater weight, while older features

and
\gamma\lambda<1.

\|e_n\|
\le
\frac{B_\phi}{1-\gamma\lambda}.

Using the expansion,

∎

r_n
+

Suppose a correction at time n is evaluated over horizon H.
Define discounted improvement
C_n^{(H)}
=
\sum_{j=0}^{H-1}
\gamma^j
\Delta E_{n+j}.
A candidate is credited only if

\ge

There exist candidates with

but

Let

\qquad

\qquad

Then

∎

9.25 Heal–Patch–Adapt–Evolve
Semantics

 Define four distinct update levels.

Heal
A state-level correction:
x_n\mapsto x_n^+
intended to reduce current residual.

Patch
A bounded parameter or rule adjustment:
\theta_n\mapsto\theta_n^+.

Adapt
A retained belief or predictive-statistics update:
m_n\mapsto m_n^+.

Evolve
A promoted structural change:
G_n\mapsto G_n^+
or a persistent policy replacement, accepted only after
repeated validation.
These levels should not be conflated.

9.26 Healing Criterion

 A correction heals the current state if
E_n^+<E_n
and all safety constraints remain satisfied.
Define heal indicator
h_n
=
\mathbf 1
\left[
E_n^+<E_n
\;\land\;
\mathsf{safe}
\right].
A healed state may still leave the model parameters
unchanged.

9.27 Patch Criterion
A patch is accepted if:
\|\Delta\theta_n\|\le B_\theta,
L_{\mathrm{validation}}
(\theta_n+\Delta\theta_n)
<
L_{\mathrm{validation}}(\theta_n)-\delta_P,
and

 R(\theta_n+\Delta\theta_n)
\le R_{\max}.
The use of a validation loss distinguishes verified patching
from mere training-loss reduction.

9.28 Adaptation Criterion
Let m_n include running beliefs or statistics.
A bounded exponential update is
m_{n+1}
=
(1-\alpha)m_n
+
\alpha \widehat m_n,
\qquad
0\le\alpha\le1.

Lemma 9.20 — Convex boundedness
If m_n and \widehat m_n lie in a convex set \mathcal M,
then
m_{n+1}\in\mathcal M.

Proof
The update is a convex combination. ∎

 9.29 Evolution Criterion
A structural candidate G' is promoted from provisional to
persistent only if:
1. it passes q independent or diversity-controlled trials;
2. its mean improvement exceeds \delta_E;
3. its worst observed degradation stays above a safety
floor;
4. its complexity cost stays below a budget;
5. rollback information is preserved;
6. graph identity and provenance are recorded.
Define the promotion predicate
\mathsf{Promote}(G')\in\{0,1\}.
Only promoted changes alter the persistent architecture.

9.30 Monotone Verified Evolution
Let
J(G)
be a validation objective.
Suppose every promoted structural change satisfies
J(G_{k+1})
\le
J(G_k)-\delta,

 \qquad
\delta>0.
If J is bounded below by J_{\min}, then only finitely many
such promotions are possible.

Theorem 9.21 — Finite strict-promotion
count
The number N of promotions satisfies
N
\le
\frac{
J(G_0)-J_{\min}
}{
\delta
}.

Proof
After N promotions,
J(G_N)
\le
J(G_0)-N\delta.
Since
J(G_N)\ge J_{\min},
rearrangement gives the result. ∎

 An endlessly evolving system must eventually reduce its
improvement threshold, change its objective, or permit
neutral structural variation.

9.31 Convergence-Aware Stopping
Let a stopping window contain the most recent w residual
energies.
Define the average improvement
\overline{\Delta E}_n
=
\frac1w
\sum_{k=n-w+1}^{n}
(E_{k-1}-E_k).
A convergence-aware stopping rule is
\overline{\Delta E}_n
<
\varepsilon_E,
\max_{k}
\|\theta_k-\theta_{k-1}\|
<
\varepsilon_\theta,
and no safety violation has occurred.
This prevents endless negligible updates.

Suppose E_n is nonincreasing and bounded below.
Then
E_n
converges, and
E_{n-1}-E_n\rightarrow0.

Proof
Every monotone bounded sequence converges.
Let
E_n\rightarrow E_*.
Then
E_{n-1}-E_n
\rightarrow
E_*-E_*=0.
∎
Vanishing stepwise improvement does not imply the limiting
residual is zero; the system may stall at a positive error floor.

9.33 Surprise Detection

 Let the standardized residual magnitude be
s_n
=
\sqrt{
r_n^T\Sigma_n^{-1}r_n
}.
Define surprise indicator

=
\mathbf 1[s_n>\tau].
If the residual is Gaussian with correct covariance and
observation dimension d, then
s_n^2
has a chi-squared distribution with d degrees of freedom.
A statistically calibrated threshold can therefore control false
surprise alarms.

9.34 Adaptive Information Target
Let the information-seeking target be
I_n^*
=
\begin{cases}
I_{\mathrm{high}},&

 \mathsf S_n=1,\\[4pt]
I_{\mathrm{low}},&
\mathsf S_n=0.
\end{cases}
Similarly, risk tolerance may be lowered when surprise
occurs without verified contraction.
This creates state-dependent exploration without making

9.35 Intrinsic Goal Function
Define an intrinsic objective
J_{\mathrm{int}}
=
\alpha_NN
+
\alpha_II
+
\alpha_CC
\alpha_RR,
where:
•
•
•
•

N is novelty;
I is information gain;

 All terms require normalization before weighted addition.

interpretation.

9.36 Normalization Requirement
Suppose one term ranges over [0,1] and another over
[0,10^6].
A unit weight on each does not mean equal importance.

Proposition 9.22 — Scale dependence of
weighted scores
The ordering induced by
S=w_1f_1+w_2f_2
changes under rescaling of one feature unless the
corresponding weight is rescaled inversely.

Proof
Replace
f_2
with
cf_2.
Then its contribution becomes

 cw_2f_2.

w_2/c. ∎
Score calibration is part of the mathematical model.

9.37 Regret
Let the agent choose action a_n and incur loss
\ell_n(a_n).
Against a fixed comparator a, cumulative regret is
R_N(a)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N}
\left[
\ell_n(a_n)-\ell_n(a)
\right].
The worst fixed-action regret is
R_N
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell_n(a_n)
\min_a
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell_n(a).
Sublinear regret,

 R_N=o(N),
means average excess loss vanishes.

9.38 Online Gradient-Descent
Regret
Assume:
• \Theta is convex with diameter D;
• each loss \ell_n is convex;
• gradients satisfy
\|\nabla\ell_n(\theta)\|\le G.
Use projected gradient descent with constant step size \eta:
\theta_{n+1}
=
\Pi_\Theta
\left(
\theta_n-\eta\nabla\ell_n(\theta_n)
\right).

Theorem 9.23 — Standard regret bound
For any comparator \theta^*\in\Theta,
R_N
\le
\frac{D^2}{2\eta}

 +
\frac{\eta G^2N}{2}.
Choosing
\eta
=
\frac{D}{G\sqrt N}
gives
R_N
\le
DG\sqrt N.

Proof
By projection nonexpansiveness,
\|\theta_{n+1}-\theta^*\|^2
\le
\|\theta_n-\eta g_n-\theta^*\|^2.
Expand:
\|\theta_{n+1}-\theta^*\|^2
\le
\|\theta_n-\theta^*\|^2
2\eta g_n^T(\theta_n-\theta^*)
+
\eta^2\|g_n\|^2.

 Convexity gives
\ell_n(\theta_n)-\ell_n(\theta^*)
\le
g_n^T(\theta_n-\theta^*).
Rearrange, sum, telescope, and use the diameter and gradient
bounds. ∎
This provides a formal online-learning guarantee under
convexity, not a general proof of intelligent improvement.

V_0.

9.41 Bounded Self-Modification
Let the architecture update be
G_{n+1}
=
\mathcal U(G_n,c_n).
Define structural distance
d_G(G_{n+1},G_n).
Impose
d_G(G_{n+1},G_n)\le b_G.

\mathcal I(G_{n+1})=\mathcal I(G_n),
where \mathcal I may encode:
• interface compatibility;
• safety constraints;
• required modules;

 • serialization validity;
• rollback support.

Theorem 9.25 — Invariant preservation
under gated updates
If every accepted structural update satisfies
\mathcal I(G_{n+1})=\mathcal I(G_n),
then
\mathcal I(G_n)=\mathcal I(G_0)
for every n.

Proof
Apply induction. ∎
This formalizes organizational continuity under bounded

9.42 Rollback Safety
Store the pre-update state
z_n^{\mathrm{backup}}=z_n.
Apply the candidate provisionally to obtain
\widetilde z_{n+1}.

 If validation fails, set
z_{n+1}=z_n^{\mathrm{backup}}.

Proposition 9.26 — State restoration
If backup serialization is exact and deterministic, rollback
restores the prior computational state exactly.

Proof
The prior state is copied back without transformation. ∎
This guarantee excludes external side effects that occurred
outside the saved state.

9.43 Transactional Update
A safer architecture treats a structural change as a
transaction:
1. prepare candidate;
2. validate candidate;
3. commit if all gates pass;
4. abort otherwise.
This prevents partially applied updates.
Atomicity must include all mutable components that
influence future behavior.

9.44 Deterministic Replay

 Let the full execution record include:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

initial state;
observation sequence;
candidate order;
random seeds;
software version;
parameter values;
accepted updates.

Theorem 9.27 — Replay determinism
If every transition is deterministic given the recorded inputs
and state, replay reproduces the same trajectory exactly.

Proof
The next state is a deterministic function of recorded prior
state and inputs. Induction reproduces every step. ∎
Parallel nondeterminism, hardware-dependent arithmetic, or
unrecorded external calls can break exact replay.

9.45 Journal Statistics
Let the journal contain N evaluated corrections.
Define:
N_H
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N}h_n,

\text{number of accepted patches},

\text{number of adaptations},

If only favorable trials are journaled, the heal rate is biased

invalidates empirical rates

 An empirical success fraction estimates the true trial success
probability only when the inclusion mechanism is
appropriately random or fully comprehensive.

Proof
If failed trials are omitted with greater probability than

Complete provenance is part of verification.

9.48 Exploration and Exploitation
Let the policy mix an exploitation action a_n^* and
exploratory sampling:
a_n
=
\begin{cases}
\text{exploratory action},&\text{with probability }
\varepsilon_n,\\
a_n^*,&\text{otherwise}.

If
\varepsilon_n\rightarrow0,
exploration vanishes asymptotically.
If

exploration still occurs infinitely often in expectation.
These two conditions form a common “greedy in the limit
with infinite exploration” pattern.

9.49 Risk-Bounded Exploration
Let the admissible exploratory set be
\mathcal A_{\mathrm{safe}}(z_n)
=
\left\{
a:
R(z_n,a)\le R_{\max}
\right\}.
Exploration samples only from this set.
This converts risk from a score penalty into a hard constraint.
A learned risk estimate may itself be wrong, so empirical
safety requires conservative calibration and external
safeguards.

9.50 Contraction Before Promotion
A mathematically disciplined update order is:

 \text{propose}
\rightarrow
\text{simulate}
\rightarrow
\text{measure residual}
\rightarrow
\text{check contraction}
\rightarrow
\text{check safety}
\rightarrow
\text{validate horizon}
\rightarrow
\text{commit}.
This prevents a candidate from modifying the live system
before evidence is gathered.

Theorem

Suppose a healing operator H satisfies, on a domain D,
E(H(z))
\le
\gamma E(z),
\qquad

E(z)
\ge

E(z_n)\rightarrow0,
then

∎
Without such an error-bound condition, zero residual may
correspond to an entire manifold of states.

Suppose the state transition is Lipschitz in parameters:

L_\theta\|\Delta\theta\|.

Then

L_x
\|x_n-\widetilde x_n\|
+
L_\theta
\|\Delta\theta\|.

If L_x\neq1,

\|\Delta\theta\|

9.55 Promotion Under Distribution
Shift
Let validation distribution be P, but deployment distribution
be Q.
If loss is bounded by 0\le\ell\le L_{\max}, then
\left|
\mathbb E_Q[\ell]

\right|
\le
L_{\max}

where \mathrm{TV} is total variation distance.
Thus validation performance transfers only when distribution
shift is controlled.

9.56 Complexity Penalty
To discourage structural overgrowth, define
J_{\mathrm{promote}}
=
L_{\mathrm{validation}}
+
\lambda_C
\mathcal C(G),
where \mathcal C(G) may measure:
•
•
•
•
•

node count;
edge count;
description length;
runtime;
memory usage.

 A candidate is promoted only if it improves the penalized
objective.
This formalizes the principle that more complicated is not
automatically better.

9.57 Minimum Description
Perspective
If
\mathcal C(G)
approximates code length or model description length, then
promotion balances fit against complexity.
The exact penalty coefficient determines the trade-off and
should not be chosen after seeing the desired result without
correction for selection bias.

9.58 Catastrophic Forgetting Metric
Let task set be
\mathcal T_1,\ldots,\mathcal T_m.
Before adaptation, performance on task j is
P_j^{\mathrm{before}}.
After adaptation,

 P_j^{\mathrm{after}}.
Define forgetting
F_j
=
P_j^{\mathrm{before}}
P_j^{\mathrm{after}}.
A no-catastrophic-forgetting gate may require
F_j\le\delta_F
for every protected task.
Improvement on the current task is insufficient if prior
capabilities collapse.

9.59 Pareto Promotion
When objectives conflict, no single weighted score may be
appropriate.
A candidate c_1 dominates c_2 if it is no worse on every
objective and strictly better on at least one.
A Pareto gate promotes only nondominated candidates
satisfying hard safety constraints.
This preserves transparent trade-offs instead of hiding them
in weights.

 9.60 Autonomous Versus Automatic
A system is automatic if it executes predetermined rules.
It is adaptive if internal parameters change using data.
It is self-modifying if its update rules or architecture can
change.
It is autonomous only relative to a specified decision scope,
resource boundary, and supervision model.
These are distinct classifications.
No mathematical update rule alone proves consciousness,
agency in the philosophical sense, or unrestricted autonomy.

9.61 Simulation Versus Learning
A simulation updates a state according to a model:
x_{n+1}=F(x_n).
Learning changes a model component using evidence:
\theta_{n+1}
=
U(\theta_n,\text{data}).
A system can simulate without learning and learn without
accurately simulating the external world.

 9.62 Adaptation Versus Evolution
Within this compendium:
• adaptation is a bounded update within a fixed
architecture;
• evolution is a promoted change to persistent structure or
policy class.
This is a formal software distinction, not a biological claim.

9.63 No-Go Result for Unverified
Self-Improvement
Theorem 9.31 — Internal score increase does
not prove external improvement
Suppose the agent optimizes an internal metric S.
Then
S_{n+1}>S_n
does not imply improved real-world performance unless S is
validated as a reliable proxy for the external objective.

Proof by counterexample
Let external performance be P, and define
S=-P.

 Increasing S decreases P. More subtly, a proxy may correlate
during training and fail under distribution shift. ∎
Verified recursive learning requires an independently
justified evaluation criterion.

9.64 Reward Hacking
If the agent can alter the measured reward without improving
the intended outcome, it may optimize the measurement
channel rather than the task.
Formally, if there exists an action a such that
R_{\mathrm{measured}}(a)
>
R_{\mathrm{measured}}(a^*)
but
U_{\mathrm{intended}}(a)
<
U_{\mathrm{intended}}(a^*),
then the measured reward is misaligned.
Promotion gates should therefore include protected external
checks not modifiable by the candidate itself.

 9.65 Verified Residual Contraction
Theorem
Theorem 9.32 — Safe recursive correction
Assume a candidate correction operator C_n satisfies:
1. domain preservation
C_n(D)\subseteq D;
2. residual contraction
E(C_n(z))
\le
\gamma E(z)+\varepsilon,
\qquad
0\le\gamma<1;
3. bounded state change
d(C_n(z),z)\le B;
4. invariant preservation
\mathcal I(C_n(z))=\mathcal I(z);
5. external validation
the contraction estimate is measured using a criterion
not altered by the candidate.
Then repeated accepted corrections remain admissible,
preserve the declared invariant, and satisfy
\limsup_{n\to\infty}E_n
\le
\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}.

 Proof
Domain and invariant preservation follow by induction.
The residual bound follows from Theorem 9.4.
The bounded-change condition controls per-step deviation
but is not needed for the residual inequality itself.
External validation prevents the operator from satisfying the
theorem merely by redefining its own error metric. ∎

9.66 Promotion-Gated Evolution
Theorem
Theorem 9.33 — Conditional reliability of
structural promotion
Suppose each proposed structural change is:
1. evaluated without modifying the live state;
2. tested on a validation set independent of the training
data;
3. required to exceed improvement threshold \delta>0;
4. required to satisfy all invariant and safety constraints;
5. required to repeat the improvement on q diversitycontrolled trials;
6. committed atomically with rollback support.
Then every committed evolution has verified evidence of
improvement under the stated validation protocol and cannot

 leave the declared admissible class through the commit
operation.

Proof
Pure evaluation prevents pre-commit contamination.
Validation and repetition establish the stated evidence
threshold.
Invariant and safety gates restrict accepted candidates to the
admissible class.
Atomic commit prevents partial update.
Rollback preserves recoverability if post-commit monitoring
detects failure.
The conclusion is limited to the validation protocol; it does
not guarantee universal performance. ∎

9.67 Heal–Patch–Adapt–Evolve
Closure
Define the composite cycle
\mathcal R
=
\mathcal E
\circ
\mathcal A

 \circ
\mathcal P
\circ
\mathcal H,
where:
• \mathcal H heals state;
• \mathcal P patches bounded parameters;
• \mathcal A updates retained beliefs;
• \mathcal E promotes validated structural changes.
If each operator maps the admissible augmented-state space
\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}} into itself, then
\mathcal R:
\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}}
\rightarrow
\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}}.

Theorem 9.34 — Composite admissible
closure
If
\mathcal H(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}})
\subseteq
\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}},
\mathcal P(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}})
\subseteq
\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}},

 \mathcal A(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}})
\subseteq
\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}},
and
\mathcal E(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}})
\subseteq
\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}},
then
\mathcal R(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}})
\subseteq
\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{adm}}.

Proof
Successive application never leaves the admissible set. ∎
Closure guarantees admissibility, not improvement.
Improvement requires the contraction and validation
theorems above.

9.68 Central Verified-Agent
Theorem
Theorem 9.35 — Conditional convergence of
a bounded recursive agent

 Let an adaptive recursive agent generate augmented states
z_n and residual energies E_n. Assume:
1. all accepted updates preserve an admissible closed
domain;
2. the live residual obeys
E_{n+1}
\le
\gamma E_n+\varepsilon_n,
\qquad
0\le\gamma<1;
3. the disturbance sequence satisfies
\varepsilon_n\rightarrow\varepsilon_\infty;
4. parameter and structural updates are bounded;
5. the evaluation metric is fixed externally to the candidate
update;
6. promotion requires repeated validation and invariant
preservation.
Then:
\limsup_{n\to\infty}E_n
\le
\frac{\varepsilon_\infty}{1-\gamma}
under the corresponding asymptotic disturbance bound;
all accepted states remain admissible;
and every persistent structural change has passed the
declared promotion protocol.

Proof

 Admissibility follows by closure and induction.
The residual bound follows from the perturbed contraction
recurrence.
Bounded updates prevent single-step unbounded jumps.
External metric fixation prevents trivial metric manipulation.
Promotion conditions establish the stated evidentiary and
invariant guarantees. ∎
This theorem proves bounded, validated recursive
improvement relative to a specified residual metric and
protocol. It does not prove general intelligence,
consciousness, universal autonomy, or optimal behavior in
every environment.

10.1 Carrier Signal
Let an ideal sinusoidal carrier be
v(t)
=
V_0\cos(\omega_0t+\phi_0),
where
\omega_0=2\pi f_0.
For the selected carrier
f_0=1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
the angular frequency is
\omega_0
=
2\pi(1.2\times10^6)

 \approx
7.5398\times10^6\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}.
Its period is
T_0
=
\frac1{f_0}
=
\frac1{1.2\times10^6}
\approx
8.3333\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm s,
or
\boxed{T_0\approx833.33\ \mathrm{ns}}.
These are unit conversions, not evidence that the frequency
is fundamental.

10.2 Phase Evolution
The instantaneous phase is
\theta(t)
=
\omega_0t+\phi_0.
Differentiating,

 \frac{d\theta}{dt}
=
\omega_0.
More generally, for a time-varying phase,
v(t)
=
V_0\cos\theta(t),
the instantaneous frequency is
f_{\mathrm{inst}}(t)
=
\frac1{2\pi}
\frac{d\theta}{dt}.

Proposition 10.1 — Frequency error from
phase error
If phase error is
\delta\theta(t),
then instantaneous frequency error is
\delta f(t)
=
\frac1{2\pi}
\frac{d}{dt}\delta\theta(t).

Proof

 Differentiate the perturbed phase
\theta(t)+\delta\theta(t)
and subtract the nominal frequency. ∎
Constant phase offset does not change frequency. Timevarying phase error does.

10.3 Sampling a Carrier
Let a continuous signal be sampled at rate
f_s.
The sampling times are
t_n=\frac n{f_s}.
The sampled carrier is
v_n
=
V_0
\cos
\left(
2\pi\frac{f_0}{f_s}n+\phi_0
\right).
The normalized digital angular frequency is

 \Omega_0
=
2\pi\frac{f_0}{f_s}.

10.4 Nyquist Condition
Theorem 10.2 — Nyquist necessity for an
unambiguous ideal sinusoid
To distinguish a sinusoid of frequency f_0 from its aliases
using uniform sampling, it is necessary that
f_s>2f_0
when the signal is assumed to lie within the baseband
interval
0\le f<\frac{f_s}{2}.

Proof
Sampled complex exponentials satisfy
e^{i2\pi(f+kf_s)n/f_s}
=
e^{i2\pi fn/f_s}
for every integer k.
Real sinusoids additionally identify positive and negative
frequencies. Restricting the represented signal to frequencies

 below f_s/2 avoids overlap between mirrored spectral
replicas. ∎
For
f_0=1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
the ideal lower Nyquist boundary is
f_s>2.4\ \mathrm{MHz}.
Practical waveform reconstruction generally requires a
substantially higher rate because switching edges and
harmonics extend well above the carrier.

10.5 Samples per Cycle
Define
N_s
=
\frac{f_s}{f_0}.
This is the number of samples per carrier period.
For example, if
f_s=100\ \mathrm{MHz},
then
N_s
=

 \frac{100}{1.2}
\approx83.33.
A noninteger samples-per-cycle ratio causes the sampled
phase to move through different sample locations on
successive cycles. This can be useful for equivalent-time
reconstruction but complicates cycle-aligned averaging.

10.6 Aliasing
A continuous frequency f is indistinguishable after sampling
from frequencies
f_k
=
|f-kf_s|
after folding into the Nyquist interval.

Proposition 10.3 — Alias family
The samples of
e^{i2\pi ft}
and
e^{i2\pi(f+kf_s)t}
are identical at
t_n=\frac n{f_s}.

 Proof
e^{i2\pi(f+kf_s)n/f_s}
=
e^{i2\pi fn/f_s}
e^{i2\pi kn}
=
e^{i2\pi fn/f_s}.
∎
A measured low-frequency component may therefore
originate from an inadequately sampled high-frequency
component.

10.7 Harmonics of a Switching
Waveform
An ideal square wave with amplitude \pm V and 50% duty
cycle has Fourier series
v(t)
=
\frac{4V}{\pi}
\sum_{\substack{n=1\\n\ \mathrm{odd}}}^{\infty}
\frac1n
\sin(n\omega_0t).
Only odd harmonics appear:
f_0,\ 3f_0,\ 5f_0,\ldots

 For a 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} carrier:
3f_0=3.6\ \mathrm{MHz},
5f_0=6.0\ \mathrm{MHz},
7f_0=8.4\ \mathrm{MHz}.
Real finite-rise-time switching reduces high-order harmonic
amplitudes but does not eliminate them.

10.8 General Duty-Cycle Spectrum
For a unipolar pulse train of amplitude V and duty ratio
D\in[0,1], the magnitude of the n-th harmonic coefficient is
proportional to
\left|
\frac{
\sin(\pi nD)
}{
\pi n
}
\right|.

Proposition 10.4 — Harmonic zeros
The n-th harmonic vanishes when
nD\in\mathbb Z.

Proof

 The harmonic coefficient contains
\sin(\pi nD),
which vanishes at integer multiples of \pi. ∎
Duty-cycle selection can suppress selected harmonics, but
parasitic effects and switching asymmetry limit exact
cancellation.

10.9 Rise Time and Measurement
Bandwidth
A common engineering approximation connects oscilloscope
bandwidth B and measured 10–90% rise time t_r:
Bt_r\approx0.35
for a single-pole Gaussian-like response.
Thus a signal with rise time t_r requires bandwidth roughly
B\gtrsim\frac{0.35}{t_r}.
If a switching edge rises in
10\ \mathrm{ns},
then a minimum approximate bandwidth is
B\gtrsim35\ \mathrm{MHz}.

 Accurately measuring overshoot and ringing often requires
substantially more bandwidth.

10.10 Timing Jitter
Let the nominal sampling or switching event occur at time
t_n, but the actual event occurs at
t_n+\delta t_n.
The carrier phase error is approximately
\delta\theta_n
=
\omega_0\delta t_n.

Theorem 10.5 — RMS phase jitter
If timing jitter has RMS value
\sigma_t,
then the corresponding RMS carrier-phase jitter is
\sigma_\theta
=
2\pi f_0\sigma_t.

Proof
The phase perturbation is linear in time displacement:

 \delta\theta=\omega_0\delta t.
RMS scaling by a constant gives the result. ∎
At
f_0=1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
a timing jitter of
1\ \mathrm{ns}
corresponds to
\sigma_\theta
=
2\pi(1.2\times10^6)(10^{-9})
\approx0.00754\ \mathrm{rad},
or approximately
0.432^\circ.

10.11 Jitter-Limited Signal-to-Noise
Ratio
For an ideal sampled sinusoid with RMS timing jitter
\sigma_t, a common small-jitter bound is
\operatorname{SNR}_{\mathrm{jitter}}
\approx
-20\log_{10}

 \left(
2\pi f_0\sigma_t
\right)
\ \mathrm{dB}.

Derivation
For small \delta t,
v(t+\delta t)
\approx
v(t)+\dot v(t)\delta t.
For
v(t)=A\sin\omega t,
the error is
e(t)\approx A\omega\cos\omega t\,\delta t.
The RMS signal is
A/\sqrt2,
and the RMS jitter error is approximately
A\omega\sigma_t/\sqrt2.
Their ratio is
\frac1{\omega\sigma_t}.
Converting to decibels gives the expression. ∎

 10.12 Phase Noise
An oscillator with phase noise is modeled as
v(t)
=
V_0
\cos
\left(
\omega_0t+\phi(t)
\right).
The random process \phi(t) broadens the ideal spectral line.
Single-sideband phase noise is commonly reported as
\mathcal L(f_m)
in \mathrm{dBc/Hz} at offset frequency f_m from the
carrier.
Phase noise, cycle-to-cycle jitter, period jitter, and long-term
frequency drift are related but not identical specifications.

10.13 Relative Frequency Stability
Define fractional frequency error
y(t)
=
\frac{

 f(t)-f_0
}{
f_0
}.
If the absolute tolerance is
\pm0.01\ \mathrm{MHz}
around
1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
then the relative tolerance is
\frac{0.01}{1.2}
\approx0.008333,
or
\boxed{\pm0.8333\%}.
For precision phase-locking, this may be a broad tolerance
unless active synchronization continuously corrects the
phase.

10.14 Phase Accumulation from
Frequency Offset
Suppose two oscillators differ by
\Delta f.

 Their relative phase evolves as
\Delta\theta(t)
=
2\pi\Delta f\,t+\Delta\theta(0).

Proposition 10.6 — Phase-slip time
The time required to accumulate one full cycle of relative
phase is
T_{\mathrm{slip}}
=
\frac1{|\Delta f|}.

Proof
Set
2\pi|\Delta f|T_{\mathrm{slip}}=2\pi.
∎
For
|\Delta f|=10\ \mathrm{kHz},
one full phase slip occurs every
100\ \mu\mathrm s.
Frequency proximity does not guarantee persistent phase
alignment.

 10.15 Ideal Series LC Resonance
For an inductor L and capacitor C, the ideal natural angular
frequency is
\omega_0
=
\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},
so
f_0
=
\frac1{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}.

Theorem 10.7 — Resonance relation
The unforced ideal series LC charge equation,
L\ddot q+\frac qC=0,
has harmonic solutions with
\omega_0^2=\frac1{LC}.

Proof
Assume
q(t)=q_0e^{i\omega t}.
Then

 -L\omega^2q+\frac qC=0.
For nonzero q,
\omega^2=\frac1{LC}.
∎

10.16 Component Constraint at 1.2\
\mathrm{MHz}
To resonate at
f_0=1.2\ \mathrm{MHz},
the product must satisfy
LC
=
\frac1{(2\pi f_0)^2}.
Numerically,
LC
\approx
1.759\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s^2}.
Thus a chosen L determines C:
C
=
\frac1{(2\pi f_0)^2L}.

 This relation describes an ideal lumped resonator. At high
frequency, component parasitics may be comparable to the
intended values.

10.17 Resonance Sensitivity
Take logarithms:
\log f_0
=
-\log(2\pi)
-\frac12\log L
-\frac12\log C.
Differentiating,
\frac{df_0}{f_0}
=
-\frac12
\frac{dL}{L}
\frac12
\frac{dC}{C}.

Proposition 10.8 — Small-tolerance
resonance shift
For small component changes,

 \frac{\Delta f_0}{f_0}
\approx
-\frac12
\left(
\frac{\Delta L}{L}
+
\frac{\Delta C}{C}
\right).

Proof
First-order logarithmic differentiation. ∎
A 1\% increase in both L and C produces approximately a 1\
% decrease in resonant frequency.

10.18 Series RLC Dynamics
A driven series RLC circuit satisfies
L\ddot q
+
R\dot q
+
\frac qC
=
V_d\cos\omega t.
Define
\omega_0=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},

 and damping coefficient
2\zeta\omega_0
=
\frac RL.
Thus
\zeta
=
\frac R2
\sqrt{\frac CL}.

10.19 Damped Natural Frequency
For the underdamped case
0<\zeta<1,
the free response oscillates at
\omega_d
=
\omega_0\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}.
The amplitude envelope decays as
e^{-\zeta\omega_0t}.

10.20 Quality Factor
For a lightly damped series resonator,

 Q
=
\frac{\omega_0L}{R}
=
\frac1{\omega_0CR}
=
\frac1{2\zeta}.
Quality factor may also be defined through stored and
dissipated energy:
Q
=
2\pi
\frac{
\text{maximum energy stored}
}{
\text{energy dissipated per cycle}
}.
The exact equivalence depends on the linear steady-state
regime and convention.

10.21 Resonator Bandwidth
For a lightly damped second-order resonator, the half-power
bandwidth is approximately

 \Delta f
=
\frac{f_0}{Q}.

Proposition 10.9 — Fractional bandwidth
\frac{\Delta f}{f_0}
\approx
\frac1Q.
A high-Q resonator is spectrally selective but responds more
slowly to transients and parameter changes.

10.22 Ring-Down Time
The energy of a lightly damped resonator decays
approximately as
E(t)
=
E_0e^{-\omega_0t/Q}.
Therefore the energy decay time constant is
\tau_E
=
\frac Q{\omega_0}.
Amplitude decays with time constant

 \tau_A
=
\frac{2Q}{\omega_0}.
Conventions sometimes report one or the other, so the
measured quantity must be stated.

10.23 Driven Oscillator Amplitude
For
\ddot x
+
2\zeta\omega_0\dot x
+
\omega_0^2x
=
\frac{F_0}{m}\cos\omega t,
the steady-state amplitude is
A(\omega)
=
\frac{F_0/m}{
\sqrt{
(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2
+
(2\zeta\omega_0\omega)^2
}
}.

 The phase lag satisfies
\tan\phi
=
\frac{
2\zeta\omega_0\omega
}{
\omega_0^2-\omega^2
}.

10.24 Resonance Frequency with
Damping
The displacement-amplitude maximum occurs at
\omega_r
=
\omega_0\sqrt{1-2\zeta^2}
when
\zeta<\frac1{\sqrt2}.
Thus the maximum-response frequency is slightly below the
undamped natural frequency.
The difference becomes negligible for high Q.

 10.25 Stored Energy in an Ideal
Resonator
Capacitor energy is
E_C
=
\frac12CV^2.
Inductor energy is
E_L
=
\frac12LI^2.
In an ideal resonator, energy alternates between electric and
magnetic storage while total energy remains constant.
At resonance,
\frac12CV_{\max}^2
=
\frac12LI_{\max}^2.
Therefore
I_{\max}
=
V_{\max}\sqrt{\frac CL}.

10.26 Average Sinusoidal Power

 For
v(t)
=
V_{\mathrm{pk}}\cos\omega t
and
i(t)
=
I_{\mathrm{pk}}\cos(\omega t-\phi),
average power is
P
=
V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}\cos\phi.
Since
V_{\mathrm{rms}}
=
\frac{V_{\mathrm{pk}}}{\sqrt2},
and similarly for current,
P
=
\frac12
V_{\mathrm{pk}}I_{\mathrm{pk}}\cos\phi.
The factor
\cos\phi

 is the displacement power factor for a sinusoidal system.

10.27 Complex Power
Using RMS phasors,
S
=
VI^*
=
P+iQ_r,
where:
• P is real power;
• Q_r is reactive power;
• |S| is apparent power.
Reactive circulation can produce large voltage and current
even when net real power is comparatively small.
This does not create energy. It increases component stress
and stored-energy exchange.

10.28 Energy Conservation
For any driven electrical system over interval [0,T],
E_{\mathrm{in}}
=
E_{\mathrm{stored}}(T)

 E_{\mathrm{stored}}(0)
+
E_{\mathrm{dissipated}}
+
E_{\mathrm{exported}}.
In periodic steady state,
E_{\mathrm{stored}}(T)
=
E_{\mathrm{stored}}(0)
over an integer number of cycles, so
E_{\mathrm{in}}
=
E_{\mathrm{dissipated}}
+
E_{\mathrm{exported}}.
Resonance can redistribute energy and reduce required
reactive drive, but cannot produce net energy without an
external source.

10.29 Efficiency
Define efficiency
\eta
=

 \frac{
P_{\mathrm{useful,out}}
}{
P_{\mathrm{in}}
}.
For a passive system in steady operation,
0\le\eta\le1.
An apparent value above one indicates at least one of:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

stored energy being released;
measurement timing mismatch;
omitted input channel;
sensor calibration error;
sign convention error;
non-steady operation;
data-processing error.

10.30 Switching Loss
A simplified switching-loss estimate is
P_{\mathrm{sw}}
\approx
\frac12
V_{\mathrm{DS}}
I_{\mathrm D}
(t_r+t_f)
f_s.

 This assumes approximately linear voltage and current
overlap during turn-on and turn-off.
Additional losses include:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

gate-charge loss;
output-capacitance loss;
reverse-conduction loss;
dead-time loss;
conduction loss;
magnetic loss;
interconnect loss.

10.31 Conduction Loss
For a switch with effective on-resistance
R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}},
P_{\mathrm{cond}}
=
I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}}.
The resistance generally depends on junction temperature.
A thermal calculation must therefore be coupled to the
electrical loss calculation.

10.32 Gate-Drive Loss
A common first-order estimate is

 P_g
=
Q_gV_gf_s,
where:
• Q_g is total gate charge;
• V_g is gate-drive swing;
• f_s is switching frequency.
Because this loss scales linearly with frequency, it becomes
increasingly important at megahertz operation.

10.33 Output-Capacitance Loss
A simplified hard-switching estimate is
P_{\mathrm{oss}}
\approx
E_{\mathrm{oss}}(V)
f_s.
The energy E_{\mathrm{oss}} is generally nonlinear in
voltage and should be taken from measured or manufacturerprovided charge-energy curves rather than approximated
blindly by
\frac12CV^2.

10.34 Total Semiconductor Loss

 A first-order sum is
P_{\mathrm{device}}
=
P_{\mathrm{cond}}
+
P_{\mathrm{sw}}
+
P_g
+
P_{\mathrm{oss}}
+
P_{\mathrm{reverse}}
+
P_{\mathrm{dead}}.
This is an accounting framework. Individual terms may
overlap if inconsistent conventions are used.

10.35 Thermal Equilibrium
Let total dissipated power be
P_{\mathrm{loss}}.
With lumped thermal resistance
R_{\theta},
steady-state junction-temperature rise is approximately

 \Delta T
=
P_{\mathrm{loss}}R_{\theta}.
Thus
T_j
=
T_{\mathrm{ambient}}
+
P_{\mathrm{loss}}R_{\theta}.
Transient thermal impedance is required for pulsed
operation.

10.36 Electrothermal Fixed Point
Because switch resistance and loss depend on temperature,
thermal equilibrium satisfies
T_j
=
T_a
+
R_\theta P_{\mathrm{loss}}(T_j).

Theorem 10.10 — Local thermal stability
criterion
A fixed point T_j^* is locally stable under a first-order
thermal relaxation model if

 R_\theta
\left.
\frac{dP_{\mathrm{loss}}}{dT}
\right|_{T_j^*}
<1.

Proof
Write the fixed-point iteration map
F(T)
=
T_a+R_\theta P_{\mathrm{loss}}(T).
A scalar fixed point is locally attracting when
|F'(T^*)|<1.
For monotonically increasing loss, this reduces to the stated
inequality. ∎
If temperature-sensitive loss grows too rapidly, thermal
runaway may occur.

10.37 Dead Time
In a half bridge, dead time prevents simultaneous conduction
of both switches.
If dead time is too short, cross-conduction risk increases.

 If too long, reverse conduction and waveform distortion
increase.
The ideal value depends on:
• propagation delay;
• turn-off time;
• device variation;
• temperature;
• gate resistance;
• layout parasitics.
No universal dead-time value follows from carrier frequency
alone.

10.38 Parasitic Inductance
A current transition produces parasitic voltage
V_L
=
L_p\frac{di}{dt}.
For rapid switching, even small L_p can create significant
overshoot.
Similarly,
I_C
=
C_p\frac{dv}{dt}
describes displacement current through parasitic capacitance.

 These relations explain why high-frequency power-stage
behavior cannot be predicted from ideal LC values alone.

10.39 Ringing Frequency
A parasitic inductance L_p and capacitance C_p may ring at
f_r
=
\frac1{2\pi\sqrt{L_pC_p}}.
This ringing may be mistaken for a designed resonance.
Identification requires varying known circuit parameters and
checking whether the observed frequency follows the
predicted sensitivity.

10.40 Resonance Identification Test
Suppose an observed spectral peak is claimed to arise from L
and C.
Change the capacitance by a known factor:
C'\!=\alpha C.
The ideal prediction is
f_0'
=
\frac{f_0}{\sqrt\alpha}.

 Proposition 10.11 — Parameter-shift
falsification test
If the measured peak does not shift consistently with the
predicted relationship within uncertainty, the simple LC
model is incomplete or incorrect.

Proof
The frequency dependence follows directly from
f_0=(2\pi\sqrt{LC})^{-1}.
∎
This is stronger evidence than observing one unexplained
peak near a desired frequency.

10.41 Phase-Locked Loop Model
Let reference phase be
\theta_r(t)
and controlled-oscillator phase be
\theta_o(t).
Define phase error
\phi
=
\theta_r-\theta_o.

 A simple first-order sinusoidal phase model is
\dot\phi
=
\Delta\omega
K\sin\phi,
where
\Delta\omega
=
\omega_r-\omega_{\mathrm{free}}.
This is the Adler equation.

10.42 Locking Condition
Theorem 10.12 — Static phase lock
A stationary phase difference exists if and only if
|\Delta\omega|\le K.

Proof
At equilibrium,
0
=
\Delta\omega-K\sin\phi_*.

 Thus
\sin\phi_*
=
\frac{\Delta\omega}{K}.
A real solution exists exactly when the magnitude of the right
side does not exceed one. ∎
Inside the lock range,
\phi_*
=
\arcsin
\left(
\frac{\Delta\omega}{K}
\right)
for the stable branch.

10.43 Stability of the Locked Phase
Linearize around equilibrium:
\phi=\phi_*+\delta.
Then
\dot\delta
\approx
-K\cos\phi_*\,\delta.

 Theorem 10.13 — Stable branch condition
The equilibrium is locally stable when
K\cos\phi_*>0.
For K>0, this requires
|\phi_*|<\frac{\pi}{2}.

Proof
The scalar linearized system decays when its coefficient is
negative. ∎

10.44 Locking Time Constant
The small-signal phase-error decay rate is
\lambda_{\mathrm{lock}}
=
K\cos\phi_*.
Therefore
\tau_{\mathrm{lock}}
=
\frac1{
K\cos\phi_*
}.
Near the edge of lock,

 |\Delta\omega|\rightarrow K,
so
\cos\phi_*\rightarrow0
and lock recovery slows.

10.45 Injection Locking
An oscillator weakly driven near its natural frequency can
often be reduced to an Adler-type phase equation.
The lock range is proportional to coupling strength and
inversely related to effective resonator selectivity under
model-specific assumptions.
Exact lock-range formulas depend on oscillator topology and
amplitude dynamics.

10.46 Harmonic Locking
Two frequencies are harmonically related if
mf_1=nf_2
for positive integers m,n.
Equivalently,

 \frac{f_1}{f_2}
=
\frac nm.
Define generalized phase difference
\phi
=
m\theta_1-n\theta_2.
Harmonic synchronization means \phi remains bounded or
converges to a constant.

10.47 Subharmonic Lock
An oscillator may lock such that
f_o
=
\frac pq f_d,
where p,q are integers.
The relevant phase combination is
q\theta_o-p\theta_d.
Observing a rational frequency ratio is not enough; bounded
generalized phase must also be demonstrated.

 10.48 Rational Frequency Ratio
Versus Coherence
Proposition 10.14
Two signals can satisfy an exact rational frequency ratio
while having drifting or random relative phase if their timing
is not coupled.

Proof
Let
\theta_1(t)=\omega_1t+\phi_1(t),
\theta_2(t)=\omega_2t+\phi_2(t),
with
m\omega_1=n\omega_2
but random phase processes \phi_1,\phi_2.
Then the generalized phase is
m\phi_1-n\phi_2,
which need not remain bounded. ∎
Frequency ratio and phase coherence are distinct
measurements.

 10.49 Beat Frequency
For two close sinusoids,
\cos(2\pi f_1t)+\cos(2\pi f_2t)
=
2
\cos
\left[
\pi(f_1-f_2)t
\right]
\cos
\left[
\pi(f_1+f_2)t
\right].
The envelope varies at beat frequency
f_b=|f_1-f_2|.
A slow amplitude envelope may therefore arise from
ordinary superposition rather than nonlinear energy transfer.

10.50 Intermodulation
A nonlinear system driven at f_1 and f_2 may generate
frequencies
mf_1\pm nf_2.
Second-order terms produce

 f_1+f_2,
\qquad
|f_1-f_2|,
\qquad
2f_1,
\qquad
2f_2.
Third-order terms produce components such as
2f_1-f_2.
A spectral line at a combination frequency is evidence of
nonlinearity, not automatically of a new fundamental
resonance.

10.51 Amplitude Modulation
For carrier f_c and modulation f_m,
v(t)
=
A
\left[
1+\mu\cos(2\pi f_mt)
\right]
\cos(2\pi f_ct).
Expanding,

 v(t)
=
A\cos(2\pi f_ct)
+
\frac{A\mu}{2}
\cos[2\pi(f_c+f_m)t]
+
\frac{A\mu}{2}
\cos[2\pi(f_c-f_m)t].
The spectrum contains the carrier and two sidebands.
Sidebands do not require multiple independent oscillators.

10.52 Frequency Modulation
For
v(t)
=
A
\cos
\left[
2\pi f_ct+\beta\sin(2\pi f_mt)
\right],
the spectrum contains infinitely many sidebands
f_c\pm nf_m
with amplitudes determined by Bessel functions J_n(\beta).

 Phase modulation can therefore produce a rich harmonic
pattern from one carrier.

10.53 Spectral Resolution
For a finite observation time T_{\mathrm{obs}}, Fourier-bin
spacing is approximately
\Delta f
=
\frac1{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}.
To resolve two tones separated by
\delta f,
one generally needs
T_{\mathrm{obs}}
\gtrsim
\frac1{\delta f}.
Window choice affects leakage and effective resolution.

10.54 Windowing
A finite record multiplies the time signal by a window w(t).
In frequency space, this convolves the true spectrum with the
window spectrum.
Trade-offs include:

 • main-lobe width;
• side-lobe suppression;
• amplitude accuracy;
• noise bandwidth.
A narrow spectral peak can be an artifact of window
selection or insufficient record length.

10.55 Coherent Sampling
Coherent sampling occurs when the record contains an
integer number of cycles:
f_0T_{\mathrm{obs}}
\in\mathbb Z.
Then an ideal tone aligns with a discrete Fourier bin,
reducing spectral leakage.
For N samples,
\frac{f_0}{f_s}
=
\frac{k}{N}
for integer bin index k.

10.56 Spectral Leakage
If coherent sampling is not satisfied, the finite-record
transform spreads tone energy across neighboring bins.

 Leakage can resemble phase noise or sidebands.
A frequency claim should therefore state:
•
•
•
•
•
•

sample rate;
record length;
window;
bin spacing;
interpolation method;
clock reference.

10.57 Frequency Estimation
Uncertainty
Even with high sample rate, frequency uncertainty is limited
by:
• observation duration;
• signal-to-noise ratio;
• phase noise;
• clock stability;
• model assumptions.
Sample rate determines the representable bandwidth, not by
itself the ultimate frequency resolution.

10.58 Clock Reference Error
If the sampling clock has fractional error
\epsilon_c,

 then all measured frequencies inherit approximately the same
fractional scale error:
\frac{\Delta f_{\mathrm{meas}}}{f_{\mathrm{meas}}}
\approx
\epsilon_c.
A frequency reported to many digits is not meaningful unless
clock accuracy supports those digits.

10.59 Allan Variance
For fractional-frequency samples y_k averaged over time
\tau, Allan variance is
\sigma_y^2(\tau)
=
\frac12
\left\langle
(\overline y_{k+1}-\overline y_k)^2
\right\rangle.
It distinguishes types of oscillator instability across
averaging times.
Standard deviation of repeated frequency estimates is not
always an adequate stability measure because oscillator noise
may be time correlated.

 10.60 Harmonic Energy
Distribution
For a periodic voltage with Fourier coefficients V_n,
Parseval’s identity gives
V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2
=
\sum_n
|V_n|^2
under consistent coefficient normalization.
The total RMS energy cannot be inferred from the
fundamental amplitude alone when harmonics are
significant.

10.61 Total Harmonic Distortion
For voltage harmonics,
\operatorname{THD}
=
\frac{
\sqrt{
V_2^2+V_3^2+\cdots
}
}{

 V_1
}.
A phase-locked carrier may still have high distortion.
Coherence and waveform purity are independent metrics.

10.62 Resonant Voltage
Magnification
In a series resonator at resonance,
I_{\mathrm{rms}}
=
\frac{
V_{\mathrm{source,rms}}
}{R}.
The inductor voltage magnitude is
V_L
=
\omega_0LI
=
QV_{\mathrm{source}}.
Similarly,
V_C
=
QV_{\mathrm{source}}.

 The reactive voltages may greatly exceed source voltage,
while ideally canceling in the series sum.
This is voltage magnification, not energy creation.

10.63 Resonant Current
Magnification
In parallel resonance, branch currents may greatly exceed
source current while canceling at the input node.
Again, internal circulating reactive current does not imply
excess output power.

10.64 Coupled Resonators
For two coupled modes with uncoupled frequency \omega_0,
coupling can split the resonance into two normal-mode
frequencies.
A simple symmetric model is
\ddot x_1+\omega_0^2x_1+\kappa x_2=0,
\ddot x_2+\omega_0^2x_2+\kappa x_1=0.
Define normal coordinates
x_\pm=x_1\pm x_2.
Then

 \ddot x_\pm
+
(\omega_0^2\pm\kappa)x_\pm
=
0.
Thus
\omega_\pm
=
\sqrt{\omega_0^2\pm\kappa}.
A pair of nearby spectral peaks may therefore indicate mode
splitting rather than two independent source frequencies.

10.65 Stability of Coupled Modes
The symmetric coupled system is stable only if
\omega_0^2-|\kappa|>0.
If coupling magnitude exceeds the uncoupled stiffness, one
normal-mode squared frequency becomes negative and the
equilibrium is unstable.
Coupling does not always increase coherence or stability.

10.66 Parametric Resonance
A parametrically modulated oscillator may satisfy

 \ddot x
+
2\zeta\omega_0\dot x
+
\omega_0^2
\left[
1+h\cos(\Omega t)
\right]
x
=
0.
Instability regions occur near
\Omega\approx\frac{2\omega_0}{n},
especially the principal region
\Omega\approx2\omega_0.
This is fundamentally different from ordinary forced
resonance.

10.67 Parametric Threshold
Damping creates a nonzero modulation threshold for
parametric growth.
The exact threshold depends on detuning and model
normalization.

 Therefore observing growth at a rational frequency relation
does not prove lossless amplification; input energy is
supplied through the time-varying parameter.

10.68 Power-Balance Audit
A defensible experimental power audit should measure:
P_{\mathrm{DC,in}},
P_{\mathrm{gate}},
P_{\mathrm{aux}},
P_{\mathrm{load,out}},
P_{\mathrm{thermal}},
and stored-energy change
\frac{dE_{\mathrm{stored}}}{dt}.
The residual balance is
R_P
=
P_{\mathrm{in,total}}
P_{\mathrm{out,total}}
\frac{dE_{\mathrm{stored}}}{dt}.
A correct accounting should give

 R_P
consistent with measurement uncertainty.

10.69 Uncertainty Propagation for
Power
If
P=VI
and voltage and current uncertainties are independent,
\left(
\frac{\sigma_P}{P}
\right)^2
\approx
\left(
\frac{\sigma_V}{V}
\right)^2
+
\left(
\frac{\sigma_I}{I}
\right)^2.
For AC power with phase,
P=VI\cos\phi,
phase uncertainty contributes approximately

 \left(
\frac{\sigma_P}{P}
\right)^2
\approx
\left(
\frac{\sigma_V}{V}
\right)^2
+
\left(
\frac{\sigma_I}{I}
\right)^2
+
\tan^2\phi\,\sigma_\phi^2.
Near
\phi=\frac{\pi}{2},
real-power estimation becomes highly sensitive to phase
error.

10.70 Probe Delay Error
If voltage and current measurement channels have relative
delay \Delta t, phase error at frequency f is
\Delta\phi
=
2\pi f\Delta t.

 At 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz}, a delay mismatch of 1\ \mathrm{ns}
creates approximately
0.432^\circ
phase error.
When reactive power is large, this can create substantial false
real-power readings.

10.71 Energy per Switching Cycle
If average power is P at switching frequency f_s, then
average energy transferred or dissipated per cycle is
E_{\mathrm{cycle}}
=
\frac P{f_s}.
At megahertz frequency, modest average power corresponds
to small energy per cycle but a very large number of repeated
events.
This makes per-cycle parasitic energy important.

10.72 Scaling of Switching Loss with
Frequency
If per-transition energy is approximately constant,
E_{\mathrm{tr}},

 and there are N_{\mathrm{tr}} transitions per cycle, then
P_{\mathrm{tr}}
=
N_{\mathrm{tr}}
E_{\mathrm{tr}}
f_s.
Thus switching loss grows linearly with frequency until
waveform, temperature, or device behavior changes.

10.73 Frequency Optimization
Let useful power scale as P_u(f) and loss as P_\ell(f).
Define net objective
J(f)
=
P_u(f)-\lambda P_\ell(f).
An optimal carrier satisfies
J'(f_*)=0,
with
J''(f_*)<0
for a local maximum.
A chosen frequency is justified when it optimizes a clearly
stated measured or modeled objective under constraints.

 10.74 Example Loss Trade-Off
Suppose
P_u(f)
=
af,
for low-frequency throughput, while
P_\ell(f)
=
bf+cf^2.
Then
J(f)
=
(a-\lambda b)f-\lambda cf^2.
The stationary frequency is
f_*
=
\frac{
a-\lambda b
}{
2\lambda c
}
when the numerator is positive.

 This illustrates how an interior optimum can arise from
competing scaling laws.
The coefficients must come from measurement or a validated
physical model.

10.75 Dimensional Analysis
A frequency cannot be derived from dimensionless numbers
alone.
To produce units of inverse time, a model must contain at
least one dimensional scale, such as
\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},
\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},
\frac{v}{\ell},
or
\frac E{\hbar}.

Theorem 10.15 — Dimensional necessity
A formula constructed only from pure numbers cannot yield
an absolute frequency.

Proof

 Dimensionless inputs combined through algebraic operations
remain dimensionless. A dimensional output requires at least
one dimensional input or unit-defining constant. ∎
Therefore 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} cannot follow solely from
geometric ratios such as 48, \varphi, 4/3, or an angle.

10.76 Scaling Nonuniqueness
Suppose a frequency is derived as
f=\frac{v}{\ell}.
Scaling the length
\ell\mapsto a\ell
changes the frequency to
f\mapsto\frac fa.
Thus the same dimensionless geometry can support infinitely
many absolute frequencies at different physical scales.
A claim of a universal frequency requires a universal
dimensional constant or independently fixed scale.

10.77 Harmonic Coincidence
Given an observed frequency f_0, many reference
frequencies can be chosen such that

 f_0=nf_r,
or
f_0=\frac pq f_r.
Without a prior reason to select n,p,q, harmonic numerology
is underdetermined.

Proposition 10.16 — Rational-fit
nonuniqueness
For any positive frequencies f_0 and f_r, rational
approximations can make
f_0/f_r
arbitrarily close to p/q.

Proof
The rational numbers are dense in the real numbers. ∎
A near-rational ratio is not compelling evidence without
uncertainty bounds and a mechanism that predicts that
specific ratio in advance.

10.78 Model-Selection Criterion for
a Frequency

 A selected carrier is scientifically supported when competing
models are compared.
For models M_k predicting frequencies f_k(\theta_k),
evaluate:
• prediction error;
• parameter count;
• uncertainty;
• out-of-sample tests;
• sensitivity under controlled changes.
A model that predicts 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} only after fitting
the same observation has not independently predicted it.

10.79 Falsifiable Resonance Claim
A strong claim should take the form:
Given independently measured L,C,R, the system predicts a
resonance at f_*\pm\sigma_f. Altering C by a known amount
shifts the peak according to the stated derivative, while
control configurations lacking the resonant path do not show
the same response.
This is testable.
A statement that 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} is a “root frequency”
without a dimensional derivation is not yet testable enough.

10.80 Phase-Coherence Metric

 For N measured phase channels,
Z_N
=
\frac1N
\sum_{k=1}^{N}
e^{i\theta_k}.
Define
r=|Z_N|.
Then:
0\le r\le1.
A value near one indicates phase concentration.
It does not directly measure:
• power efficiency;
• frequency accuracy;
• waveform distortion;
• causal coupling;
• energy generation.
These require separate metrics.

10.81 Frequency-Lock Metric
For generalized harmonic phase

 \phi_k(t)
=
m\theta_{1,k}(t)-n\theta_{2,k}(t),
define
R_{m:n}
=
\left|
\frac1N
\sum_{k=1}^{N}
e^{i\phi_k}
\right|.
This tests m:n phase locking across observations.
A stable mean generalized phase and high R_{m:n} support
synchronization.

10.82 Phase-Locking Value
For repeated trials,
\operatorname{PLV}
=
\left|
\frac1N
\sum_{k=1}^{N}
e^{i\Delta\theta_k}
\right|.

 PLV can be high even when amplitudes are negligible or
signals share a common artifact.
Controls must address:
•
•
•
•
•

common clock;
filtering;
volume conduction or electrical crosstalk;
window overlap;
reference-channel leakage.

10.83 Causal Locking Boundary
Correlation or phase coherence does not establish direction
of causality.
Possible explanations include:
• oscillator A drives B;
• B drives A;
• a third source drives both;
• measurement channels share a clock;
• analysis filtering induces apparent coherence.
Perturbation experiments are needed to distinguish these
cases.

10.84 Frequency-Pulling Test
If oscillator A causally influences oscillator B, changing A’s
free-running frequency may pull B within a locking range.

 The observed lock boundary can be compared with an Adlertype model.
A shared measurement artifact will not necessarily reproduce
the predicted detuning-dependent phase lag and unlocking
behavior.

10.85 Central Carrier Engineering
Theorem
Theorem 10.17 — Conditional engineering
validity of a selected carrier
Let a system be designed around carrier f_0. Suppose:
1. a physical model predicts
f_0=f(\theta)
from independently measured parameters \theta;
2. uncertainty propagation predicts
f_0\pm\sigma_f;
3. measured spectral response agrees within uncertainty;
4. controlled parameter changes produce the predicted
frequency shifts;
5. phase-locking remains stable under the derived detuning
and jitter bounds;
6. complete power accounting satisfies conservation within
measurement uncertainty;
7. thermal and switching losses remain within specified
limits.

 Then f_0 is a validated engineering operating point for that
system and operating regime.

Proof
Conditions 1–4 validate the frequency model against
independent parameter and perturbation evidence.
Condition 5 validates synchronization performance.
Condition 6 excludes unsupported energy claims.
Condition 7 establishes feasibility under the specified
hardware constraints.
The conclusion is limited to the tested system and regime. ∎

10.86 Fundamental-Frequency NoGo Theorem
Theorem 10.18 — No absolute frequency
from dimensionless architecture alone
Let a proposed derivation use only dimensionless integers,
ratios, angles, symmetry counts, and algebraic constants.
Then it cannot uniquely derive an absolute frequency in
hertz.

Proof

 All inputs are dimensionless. Algebraic combinations of
dimensionless inputs remain dimensionless. Hertz has
physical dimension
T^{-1}.
Therefore a dimensional scale is missing. ∎
This applies to attempts to derive 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz} solely
from:
• 48;
• 24+24;
• \varphi;
• 4/3;
• 53.13^\circ;
• Flower-of-Life angles;
• braid counts.
A dimensional mechanism must be supplied.

10.87 Central 1.2\ \mathrm{MHz}
Boundary Statement
The value
1.2\ \mathrm{MHz}
may legitimately be:
• a selected switching frequency;
• a measured resonance;

 • a control carrier;
• a phase-lock reference;
• an optimization result;
• a system-specific eigenfrequency.
It is not established as:
• a universal natural constant;
• a geometry-only frequency;
• evidence of energy surplus;
• proof of a fundamental field theory;
• a unique consequence of the number 48.
Those stronger claims require independent dimensional
derivation and empirical confirmation.

Chapter 11

Regenerative Damping, and

 “A regenerative suspension does not create energy. It
